your ruling would be. But I did not do so.
I gave the information asked for that is on the records. I should like to know from the leader of the opposition what his explanation is with regard to those figures.

I will tell the minister at once, and the answer may not meet the minister's wishes. I think the answer is that the whole selective service machinery has fallen down so far as farm labour is concerned, and1 if the minister would only admit it he would say the same himself.

Since the minister is a member of the man-power committee of the cabinet, I think he should have gone farther in answering the question asked by my colleague the leader of the opposition.
I had some difficulties in my province at Easter, and I am satisfied from what the Minister of Labour himself has said that selective service is not functioning as it should, especially in regard to agriculture. When I asked him a question the other day about it he said that I should get in touch with the selective service officer in the city of Winnipeg, that he would be able to tell me. I know some of the difficulties between the selective service officer and the draft board which calls men up, and the difficulty at that time was with conscientious objectors whose help the farmers wanted with their seeding. But the selective service officer did not have any records. The files were with the staff of the draft board. There is clearly confusion and misunderstanding between the respective authorities, and selective service is not working as it should. True enough, we have statements issued every once in a while and orders in council passed, but actually to date they have not amounted to much more than words. The minister is on the manpower committee of the cabinet and is responsible for agriculture, and even if it were not strictly in order he should discuss this question in the committee. When we raise the question with the Minister of Finance he does not know anything about it, and while the Minister of Labour is responsible for selective service he does not know agriculture as the minister does. Therefore, I think the Minister of Agriculture should enlighten us. We may get through the spring season without much help, but it will not be long before men will be needed for haying and harvest, and many farmers are already worrying how they will get off their crops if they have an average crop this year. Surely the minister should give us not only information but a lead in this matter.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Minister of Agriculture has raised the same point of order that he brought to the attention of the committee yesterday. He mentioned a fact which every member of the committee knows, namely, that the minister is always willing to answer any questions pertaining to his department; but no one should take objection to the fact that it is for the minister who is in the best position to do so to make statements and answer questions, and that the matter of manpower should be dealt with by the Minister of Labour. In my opinion the point of order was well taken, and I would ask the committee to act accordingly.

Mr. Chairman, I quite agree with what you have said, that the Minister of Agriculture is not directly responsible in this matter of man-power. Nevertheless, he is responsible for agricultural production, and agricultural production is definitely tied up with the amount of man-power available for that purpose. I think that, as a member of the man-power committee of the cabinet, he must assume a certain amount of responsibility in that regard. For that reason members of the committee should be allowed to express their views on the subject, so that the minister will have those views before him in deciding on the matter.
The other day the Minister of National Defence stated that 80 per cent of the men from agriculture who applied for postponements were granted them. I point out that that is a statement which is entirely misleading to the people of this country. True, such men may have been granted their first postponement, but in a great number of cases it was only for a short period, maybe a month, or two, or three months, and at the end of that period they were not granted a second postponement and are now in the armed forces. That point should be looked into.
I believe that to-day we have set up in Canada war production committees in most of the provinces. I know that has been done in western Canada. In many instances those committees recommend that men be granted postponements, but frequently such postponements are not granted by the board. The war production committees which have been set up both in United States and in Great Britain have been given a great deal more authority than the Canadian committees which, as I understand, have only advisory functions. I should like to give the committee an idea of the authority conferred upon war production committees in Great Britain. I read from the issue, dated May 15, of the Commercial
Supply-Agriculture

Intelligence Journal, published under the authority of the Minister of Trade and Commerce:
Too much credit for this increased productivity and general efficiency of British agriculture cannot be given to the county war agricultural executive committees. Their only "terms of reference" that mean anything are "responsibility for the production of more food." Unencumbered by red tape and clothed with authority, they have approached their problems with direptnes and understanding. They have not hesitated to advise, prescribe, and, where necessary, evict, in order to reach their goals. Their achievements speak for themselves, and it would be surprising if some similar organizations, with modified powers, were not demanded^ by British farmers in the post-war period.
I have two suggestions to make to the minister with regard to this man-power problem. When war production committees recommend that men should be placed in agriculture, their recommendations should be mandatory upon the boards which are calling those men; otherwise there is very little use in the recommendations being made. We have come to a point in the man-power situation on the farms when more drastic action must be taken. The other recommendation I would make is that men allotted to agriculture by these boards should be allotted permanently except in the event of national emergency. At the present time postponements are granted for only short periods, say three or six months; the boy goes back to the farm, and neither his father nor himself has any idea whether another postponement will be granted. Consequently they do not plan to produce more agricultural commodities. If postponements were granted with the understanding that they were permanent except in a case of national emergency, we would get a much greater production than we have at the present time.
As regards the figures of placements in agriculture which the minister has given us, I know from personal experience that, at least in Saskatchewan, they are not at all indicative of the actual requirements in the matter of labour. We have selective service offices in certain of the larger towns, but only farmers living in the neighbourhood of those towns make application there. I would say that seventy-five per cent of the farmers in Saskatchewan-and I think this is true of most of the other provinces-have never made use of these various offices. For that reason I do not regard the minister's statements as indicative of the true situation.
The minister has a responsibility with regard to this matter of man-power. I am sure he realizes the conditions. He has been in every province and probably has a much wider

knowledge of the subject than many private members, and I think he should, in his dealings with the man-power committee, take a firmer stand on behalf of agriculture. We can say that we need man-power in the army, in industry and in the navy, but neither the army, the navy nor industry will function very long on an empty stomach. We could have the best trained army in the world, but if we gave them nothing to eat for a week they would not be able to beat a second-rate armv. We may be approaching that position; we may be closer to it than we now realize. Last year Canada had the largest crop which has ever been produced, not only in this country but in the United States or the whole north American continent. Despite that fact there are shortages to-day, and in view of the lateness of the spring there is every indication that Canada and the whole of North America will have a short crop this year. As a matter of fact, the winter wheat crop of the United States is several million bushels less than it was last year. We must pay some attention to these matters before it is too late.

There is just one thing I might say, in addition to what I have already said, with regard to the figures which have been presented. To an extent, of course, the figures based on the 1941 census must be estimates. The figures with regard to the placements are actual figures, and the figures with regard to the applications which are in the offices are also actual figures. I scarcely agree with those who seem to feel that the figures do not mean anything. As a matter of fact, I had the privilege of administering the employment offices in Saskatchewan over a five-year period. Employment offices in the provinces are not a new thing; they have been established since around the end of the last war; they were set up under legislation which was passed here, if I remember rightly, in 1919, and I do not think there are many farmers anywhere in Canada who do not know that they exist. They are the same offices as are now functioning for selective service. I believe every hon. member knows where they are located in the various provinces; certainly hon. members from Saskatchewan know where they are located in their respective areas, our province being almost exclusively agricultural.
What these figures do mean is that people have not been sufficiently anxious about the employment situation on their farms to appeal to the employment offices to a greater extent than they have done. They have been directed to do so by everyone who has been talking to

Supply-Agriculture
them about these matters. I am sure that members have directed them to do so, as I have done every time they have written to me inquiring about the matter, and I have also directed them to do so publicly. I have asked those who are short of labour to apply to these offices for any assistance which can be given them, and the farmers have been applying to the offices over a long period of years, since about 1919 at least. I am sure, therefore, that some of them would apply this year if they found it necessary, and the figures which were given are figures as represented on the records of the different employment offices across Canada on April 29, 1943. Members are in as good a position to determine what that means as I am. The fact that we have had offices set up across Canada for a long term of years and that people have been accustomed to apply there if they need additional labour speaks for itself.
I agree with what is said by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), that farmers do not of necessity go there under ordinary circumstances because they employ labour in their local community. If one farmer in peace time has more sons than he needs on his own farm, a. neighbour employs a son off his farm. If there are a number of people who are ready to work on a farm, people in villages round about, they are employed on farms and therefore do not go to the employment offices. But whenever there has been a difficulty which has become serious w7ith the farmer, the practice has been to apply to the offices. Any member can arrive at his own conclusion as to why they have not done so on this occasion. I read an explanation this morning which came from a man who was very closely associated with the work in western Canada and who is doing everything he can to assist the farmers in getting men on their farms, and his explanation is this. He said: "I can scarcely understand it myself, because there has been so much complaining about the shortage of labour, and I do not see why there have not been more applications. I can only offer one of two explanations. The first is that men may be asking wages that are too high and the farmer has simply made up his mind that he cannot pay so much and that he will have to do the work as best he can with such labour as he has on his farm, and is therefore proceeding to do so." He said that might be one explanation. He said that another explanation may be that the farmers have come to the conclusion that they will have to put forth an extraordinary effort owing to the fact that we are at war, and that therefore they are
getting on with as little labour as possible and are doing the best job they can under the circumstances.
I am not in a position to say, as the hon. member for Melfort has suggested, that this will result in greatly reduced production this year. The statistics indicate that wheat seeding is down about twenty per cent. That indication was there before the weather had anything to do with the situation, or at any rate, if it had, it had little to do with it. The farmers apparently decided to follow the request made of them, which has been set out in the objectives for Canadian agriculture for 1943, and they are reducing their wheat acreage, if the bureau of statistics information is correct, by just about the amount they were asked to reduce it in this programme, namely, by something in the neighbourhood of four million acres. That would be helpful1 in getting the work done this year which they intended to do, as hon. members from the west know.
The seeding season for coarse or feed grains extends over a longer period than the seeding season for wheat. The suggestion comes from the western provinces, from those who are keeping close check on these things, that farmers will get their seed in this spring with the labour they have. I cannot give the committee anything more than the information that is given to me by the people who are keeping the records, the people who are associated with the provincial governments as well as federally, because these offices over a period of years have been operated on a fifty-fifty basis under the provinces and the federal government, and the officials have been men who have been satisfactory to both federal and provincial governments. When these men make reports we are inclined to accept them. They are based upon the experience of men.
In Saskatchewan it is reported that in addition to getting their seeding under way, and in spite of the fact that there has been some difficult weather lately, seventy-five per cent of the grain left over last fall had been threshed before we entered upon this week, and the prediction was that it would be all cleaned up by the end of the week. In Alberta the story was that sixty' per cent of the grain had been threshed and would be cleaned up by the end of the week. We have to take the reports of the people who are on the ground. I was there myself during the Easter vacation, and I found seeding well under way. Since that time I have had no information in the matter apart from what comes to us through the officials on the ground, and the report is to the effect I have indicated.
Supply-Agriculture

I may say to those who come from Ontario that this morning I read the records and found that the production of butter in that province is up twenty per cent. It is true that the production of cheese is down somewhat, but the production of butter is up twenty per cent, and I think I am correct in saying that the production of milk is not down. So that this would not suggest that the work is not being done by someone. We may argue that old people who should not be working are at work and that people who are too young to work are also working, and we can understand such arguments. After all, however, we have to take the facts as they are indicated to us in the reports that are made from time to time on what is being actually done, and we have to face those facts. When we face those facts we can probably arrive at some conclusion as to why the figures are as they are.
It is a little difficult to make comparisons such as were made by the hon. member for Melfort with regard to the situation in Britain and in Canada and derive much benefit therefrom. As I understand it, between five per cent and ten per cent of the people of Great Britain are on farms, and the organization of a farming community of that kind, in an area as small as Britain, is one thing, while the organization of a farming community in an area where thirty-seven per cent of the people are actually living on the farms and are spread across a country as great as Canada, is an entirely different thing. In the country to the south of us conditions are a little more akin to ours, but I do not find there that the complaints are any less than they are here; and in some respects I did not find, even on the other side of the ocean, that the complaints were very different in Britain from those we hear in this country. They are based on the same ideas and the same thoughts. I have in my hand a copy of the Saturday Evening Post of January 30, 1943, and I should like to read a paragraph from an article written by a well-known middle-class fanner in the eastern part of the United States. His name is Ed Will, and he writes regularly for publications of this kind. He has this to say:
A recent instruction to local selective service boards suggests deferment for farmers or farm labourers only if they are directly responsible for sixteen war units-a war unit to consist of one milk cow, or seventy-five hens, fifteen acres of hay or grain, five acres of corn or beans, twenty hogs, or other quantities of sheep, beef cattle, and so on, which may vary according to the conditions under which they are kept.
He goes on to make this comment:
Most of these units are excessively high for the northeast.

That is the northeast United States.
I found in a canvass of my own neighbourhood that the average number of units per man was eleven. The average work week rvas about sixty hours. According to that, a farmer of this locality would have to work nearly ninety hours a week to be eligible for deferment.
He goes on for a whole page to analyse what is going on in the United States where they have selective service boards and where they are presumed to have the system developed to a very high degree. Nevertheless farmers there do not find that it fits in with conditions in one part of the country as compared with another. He says it may work in Kansas, but it does not work in the northeastern part of the United States. Agriculture in Canada extends from the Pacific to the Atlantic. It may be useful for us to talk about what they do in Britain, but I think it is unreasonable to try to apply the same thing in Canada and try to make it work all across the country. As has been described by the hon. member for Melfort, committees have been set up in Saskatchewan. I think that is the first province in which they have been set up to cover the entire province. I believe the plan they have followed is being adopted by selective service, and others elsewhere are being urged to follow it. I understand that in Saskatchewan production committees under the agricultural department have been set up and that this has been utilized by selective service, in connection with man-power problems. These boards are giving advice.
May I suggest that the effectiveness of the call-up for the army under selective service is scarcely a matter that could1 properly be discussed under my estimates, even though I may be a member of the man-power committee. Even if I knew the facts, it would not be proper for me to discuss them. The proper person to discuss this matter is either the Minister of National Defence, whose estimates are before the committee and will be up for discussion the early part of next week, or the Minister of Labour, whose estimates will be before the committee. Both of these ministers will have complete information, which I . have not. Even if I had, I should not discuss the matter at this time. The proper time to discuss it is under their estimates.

In spite of what the minister says, that the subject of manpower ought not to be discussed now, I do feel that the manner of the presentation of the war appropriation measure has been altogether wrong. Man-power should have been

Supply-Agriculture
taken up first. One problem that faces Canada to-day, one thing that requires immediate consideration is the matter of selective service and the man-power situation in general. Our situation is such, that everything that Canada can contribute depends upon the solution of man-power distribution.	The
necessary men must be obtained for the army and they must be obtained for industry and for agriculture. I think the Minister of Labour should be here to give us information about the situation which now prevails in Canada in connection with agriculture.
The minister has given certain figures today, and no one can argue that those figures were not submitted by the various selective service boards across the dominion. They represent the number of applications that have been made for agricultural help from the Atlantic to the Pacific. I noticed the restraint with which the Minister of Agriculture accepted those figures. There is not a member of this house who does not realize that in no vray do they represent the situation in agriculture in so far as man-power is concerned. The number of men required on the farms in Saskatchewan is given as only 142, based on the unfilled orders as of the date of the order. In Ontario there were 1,802 unfilled orders. If those figures represent' the facts as found to exist under selective service administration, then, as the leader of the opposition has stated, a deplorable situation exists in selective service.
The minister has advanced two hypotheses as an explanation for the smallness of the figures. I think the real reason was that farmers all over Canada realized that it was no use going to the selective service board and putting in their names. They realized that if there were 1,800 or 400 or 200, as the case may be, orders still unfilled, they would not get any workers. The problem of man-power in agriculture is connected with the problem of manpower in the army and in industry. The situation cannot be as is shown by those figures, otherwise the Minister of Labour would not have found it necessary to have an order in council passed on May 4 requiring barbers, beauticians and other types of workers to register so that they might be available for transfer into agriculture on and after May 19. No matter how we endeavour to avoid facing this problem, this house will have to face it. The minister does not indicate that he expects production to be equal to what it was last year. I know that the situation, generally speaking, in western Canada-
I did the last time I spoke a week or so ago, but I did not to-day.

The situation is quite serious. There are two main pulls on man-power in addition to the attraction of the munition factories and the like, but it has had very little to do with the situation now prevailing in western Canada, for very few men and women left the farms in order to go into industry. The first pull is that of voluntary service, and the second is the administration of conscription for service in Canada, in which there has been no uniformity of application anywhere in the dominion. In some of the western provinces men have been called up from farms, leaving no one there except the old people. Regulations have been passed by the department; orders in council have followed one another in rapid succession since March 24, 1942, but orders in council, regulations and determinations of policy by the Department of Labour in collaboration with the Department of Agriculture and the various other departments mean nothing unless they are carried into effect. So far as granting postponement to men required in agriculture is concerned, the record across Canada has been this. The regulations provide for postponement, but until very recently in the administration of those regulations postponement has in many instances not been granted. The administration of the national service regulations and of conscription for service in Canada has been based on the desires and wishes of the local boards, while the agricultural representatives appearing before some of those boards have not received the consideration to which they are entitled.

We.do not even have one
in Saskatchewan.
Oh, yes, we have.
I will let the minister argue that with the hon. member for Mel-fort, but if there is one he has been unable to carry out his duties.
Oh, yes, he has.

All one has to do
is to look at the records, but I will admit that recently the situation has changed for the better. In some provinces practically every man engaged in agriculture has been granted postponement. In other provinces the situation has been that twenty-five to thirty-five per cent of those engaged in agriculture have obtained postponement. It all comes back to the fact that there is no uniformity in the application and administration of the National Resources Mobilization Act. It is administered according to the wishes of the board in each province, with no appeal possible and no control by the government over the
Supply-Agriculture

orders issued by those boards. Ia various parts of western Canada we find that farming is being carried on by men- and women advanced in years, whose sons have enlisted while others have been taken from the land and- put into the army for the defence of Canada. No one can seriously say to-day that these men- are necessary in Canada for that purpose. They have been taken out of agriculture, away from active production and placed- in- the army for the defence of Canada, but the work they are doing, unless they go overseas, cannot compare in importance with the work they would- have done had they been kept on the farms and permitted to continue production.
This problem has to be faced. The figures placed on record- to-day demonstrate the deplorable situation- in regard- to the administration- of selective service in this country. We have the set-up; we have boards all over the dominion, but there is no guidance or direction on the part of the government because it lacks a plan as to what Canada's effort shall be. We should- have a plan to show how many men are required for the armed forces, how many will be required in industry and how many must be placed- in agriculture in order to assure the production that is required of Canada. Until we have such a plan, selective service and its administration will be just a sham and a fantasy. I am not condemning the Minister of Agriculture, though we do not often see eye to eye. He has a plan for agriculture; he has stated that plan, and the farmers are endeavouring to carry it out. The trouble is that some of the other ministers have no plan with reference to Canada's war effort.
On May 4, 1943, the government finally decided- that the only way to solve this problem of labour was by adopting compulsion. In other words, the government turned its back on the voluntary system, so far as labour is concerned, and- went a step farther than it had ever gone before, by bringing into effect compulsion with regard- to labour as it previously had- brought in compulsion for service in the army for the defence of Canada. Lacking to-day is cooperation between the various ministers, to the end that agriculture, industry and the armed forces may receive their proper allocation. We have had registrations galore; there have been at least five since the national registration of 1940. Yet to-day the minister says that these are the best figures he can give, although based- on surmises and estimates. If the government wants to find- out the labour situation in agriculture to-day-and- I advance this as a serious and constructive

suggestion-secure the registration of the labour needs of the farmers of Canada. It will not cost anything, having the set-up of a selective service organization in every part of the country. Specify a date when the farmers may register their needs, so that the * labour position in regard to farm production will be correctly ascertained. I suggest that the figures obtained by such a registration will bear no resemblance whatever to the figures that have been presented- to-day I am sure there is not a member of the house, much less the minister, who would say that from the Atlantic to the Pacific only 4,250 men are required on the farms of this country. All those figures mean is that the farmers have reached the point where they realize that it is no use applying for help. They mean, too, that man-power is not in the right place at the right time. While the minister seems hopeful that production will be kept up, those with whom I have spoken invariably tell me that it will be impossible for them to keep up their production unless they are assured by the government of a supply of labour at the right time, and in particular at seeding and- at harvest.

Mr. Chairman, I should like at this time to make one or two observations respecting agriculture. May I state particularly my views as to what I think the situation is in Ontario.
Time and again we have listened to the repeated criticism of some hon. members, and especially the hon. member for Lake Centre, who repeats and repeats the same thing, day after day. I have noticed, too, that the farmers from Ontario are rather modest in expressing their views respecting the farm situation. In spite of the fact that Ontario is not supposed to be a great farming community, let me say that agricultural production in Ontario is as great as that of the three western provinces combined. But we do not do as much talking as do some of the western members, particularly one or two, who make a sorry spectacle of themselves. We, in Ontario, have not so much time to talk; we are directing our efforts to production.
The farm labour problem, as I see it, is caused by the circumstances of war, and nothing else. If conditions in agriculture were anything different from what they are, our war effort in Canada would not be the kind Mr. Churchill would comment favourably upon as he did in his speech at Washington only a few days ago. If we had any other condition different from the one we have, the situation would be distressing, in so far as measuring Canada's contribution to the war is concerned.

Supply-Agriculture
Does the hon. member for Lake Centre think we can win the war without sacrifice? Does he really think there is any element of society in this country, including farmers, which is not prepared to make sacrifices for this great cause? May I tell the committee that young farmers resent being continually described as wanting sympathy. The young farmer would like to enlist. The boys who are staying on the farms are real soldiers, doing a real job. My experience has been that, in respect of many applications for postponements, the initiative has been taken by the father, and quite properly so. In many instances the boy himself will not sign an application for postponement. I think it will be found in the majority of the applications that the boys themselves, in their quiet and modest way, have wanted to do their bit, and have refused to sign applications, or place such applications before the board for postponements.
I have found that Mr. Irwin, in military district No. 2, has been reasonable and fair so far as postponements are concerned. True, errors will be made, and sometimes poor judgment will be used. But in the main I believe that if cases have been legitimate, if applications have been made at the right time, and if the applicants have fulfilled their obligations when called up, proper consideration has been given.
That does not mean to say that we have not a real problem on our farms, and nobody knows that better than I do. But what has caused it? A good deal of that condition has been, caused by the publicity and agitation of the men who are complaining to-day about circumstances w'hich they have more or less created.
When war broke out, what was .our chief difficulty? Time and again we had tried to sell the overproduction of our farms. That had developed into a grave issue. We heard talk then about the poor farmer who had so much products he could not sell. Those who were complaining were then holding up their hands in holy terror for the distressed farmer, and complaining about overproduction. Then it developed that we needed tanks, guns and ammunition, because our farms would not be much good if we did not have the weapons of war with which to protect them. Therefore, through the wisdom of this government we allowed and encouraged men to go into industry to manufacture those things required for the protection of our country.
May I ask my hon. friend, w'ho has been so anxious to criticize, if he would have said to the farmer, "No, you must stay on the
farm; you cannot take advantage of this prosperity. This is to be enjoyed only by people living in the cities." What would have been the answer? There was a surplus of labour on the farms at that time. They took advantage of it, and1 tried to improve their financial condition. And the financial condition of the farmer has been improved, despite the fact that there are still poor people on the farms.
There has been such an increase in production that in 1942 we had the largest agricultural production in our history, despite the number of boys who have left the farms. I should like to see a survey of how many of those boys are now in the armed forces, and how many have left the farms to go into industry. That information would be most interesting. And, despite the fact that we have had difficulty on our farms in keeping our young men, the reports of mortgage companies show that farmers have been paying off their mortgages. The report of the loan and mortgage association proves that last year nine per cent of the principal sum was paid off on mortgages they hold in Canada.
The farmer who knows his business does-not need advice from some who have been offering it. He knows his job, and we should let him do the job he is capable of doing, and let others do their jobs. That is the purpose of selective service. Probably we shall make a pretty fair job of it, even if we do not receive so much advice from those who dto not know what they are talking about. The farmer is a reasonable man.
Professor Wood!
What is the hon. member looking at?

I thought someone was murmuring something. The farmer is, of course, the victim of weather conditions. One farmer said to me, "I asked you a month ago if it were possible to get a man, but I am glad I did not get that man because, with this wet weather, I would have been a nervous wreck if I had had a man sitting round1 doing nothing, at $50 a month, when we could not get on the land."
