Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at six o'clock I was endeavouring to give some reasons for the unrest in the country regarding man-power. I pointed out
Supply-Agriculture

that the man-power situation was a result of the war. I do not believe it is wisdom on the part of any government to impose compulsion in a country like Canada whose people always have prided themselves on the liberty they enjoy, and it was most amusing to hear the hon. member for Lake Centre suggest that we should have to apply compulsion. I know it would be the height of his ambition to see such a stupid thing applied because we all know how the country would take to methods of that kind.
I would say to those who criticize the man-power situation that the wrhole thing resolves itself into this. There is no manpower muddle. The only muddle is among the critics of this government who have not been able to stick consistently to one line of criticism but have endeavoured continually to create suspicion. When the war broke out, the critics of the opposition said: Get all the recruits you can into the army. There has never been a well-balanced critical attitude among the opposition, and I include all parties opposite. Had we yielded to their criticism at the outbreak of the war, we would 'have had every available man swept into the army regardless of whether he had anything to fight with or not. That would have been national suicide. Later on we had the spectacle of the committee of two hundred in Toronto which was more responsible than anything else for creating the agitation that brought about the plebiscite. They demanded an all-out war effort. But that line of criticism stuck for only three or four months, and the critics then found it necessary to raise a new argument. So that this year they say there is a man-power muddle.
The fact is that there are not enough men in the country-that is the whole trouble. The muddle is among the opposition, in their criticism which seeks to exaggerate the situation. I have no objection to people grumbling. We farmers, in Canada especially, have the British background. No one likes to grumble more than the British. It is a characteristic of them to meet and grumble at Hyde Park. But in spite of all the grumbling we farmers do we carry on in a fashion that amazes people by our accomplishments. Since the outbreak of war, agricultural production in this dominion has steadily increased, not only in dollars and cents value but in actual volume of production. From past experience we would not have much justification for accepting the arguments and views put forward by the opposition regarding the conduct of this

war. I remember the phrase that was used by a public servant of this country, a premier of one of the provinces, when the plebiscite was before the public. The phrase that he used was, "crowning indignity". He took very strong exception to the plebiscite.
We are up against a very serious problem, and it is time that we faced the facts. The farmer has a job to do and he needs encouragement. It should not always be pointed out that he is the under-dog. You can discourage a man by keeping him in a low stratum of society until he begins to lose respect for himself.
I noticed an article in the Financial Times of Montreal recently showing that the farmers in Saskatchewan, where the hon. member for Lake Centre comes from, are enjoying a fair measure of prosperity. I welcome that. But agricultural production must be associated with this prosperity. The article says that there were 3,117 discharges of rural mortgages in Saskatchewan in 1942. It does not indicate a very serious condition of affairs when that number of mortgages can be discharged in spite of the man-power muddle which hon. gentlemen opposite suggest exists and the shortage of help. If we are to win this war, there are bound to be shortages in almost every department of our economic life. Right in Brantford we have industries that need a thousand men, and I do not hear any particular complaint, or one to champion the cause of those industries, but the man-power shortage is just as serious to them as it is to the farmer. I am inclined to think that these paid grumblers for the farmers who are not farmers themselves have some ulterior motive. Perhaps they think that if we get too much production they will get cheap food, and they are not too much concerned about the future. I should like to see some of our agricultural surpluses wiped out and the farmer in a position where he will always have a market for everything he produces. He has such a market at the present time, but I should like to see him maintained in that position so that along with other walks of society he could be assured of a fair exchange of services for his efforts. I feel suspicious when I see people who are not farmers showing such an anxiety for the farmers' welfare and wanting more production. I am just a bit suspicious that they are taking a long viewpoint, hoping they will be able to get their food cheap, regardless of whether the farmer gets anything out of it or not.
The controls which we have to-day we must accept. But when it comes to sacrifice, there are those who do not mind the controls

Supply-Agriculture
so long as the other fellow does the sacrificing. That attitude just does not work in an all-out war effort, which is what the opposition has been asking for. Now when they have an all-out war effort, they are not satisfied. If we had taken the advice of the opposition things would have been in a far worse state than they are to-day. The government in its administration of the affairs of this country and in its conduct of Canada's part in the war has not been carried away by clamour, but has followed a consistent policy working toward an ideal. We have got to the place now where there is no unemployment in this dominion. If I were inclined to criticize the government, or to suggest something by way of solution of our man-power problem, I am frank to say I would advise them that there are young men in the army who, after getting their basic training, might well, instead of sitting round in the camps, go back home and help their fathers and mothers on the farms. If an effort were made to persuade some of these men to volunteer for farm work, we would get the best type of help, and give a national service which it will be impossible to give in any other way.
But compulsion is entirely another matter. It is suggested that we should compel men to leave other industries, or even the army, and force them on to the farms. I would say to the hon. member for Lake Centre that in making that suggestion he just does not know what he is talking about. It is like every other argument that I have noticed he puts up.
Mr. Chairman, will the hon. gentleman permit a question?
I am very glad to.

What is the effect
of the order in council of May 4, if it is not that very thing?

Well, the point is this. The
hon. member says it is not working, and I will agree that it is impossible. You can put men on the farm, but you cannot compel them to farm. Take some lads who have even been raised on the farms; try to compel them to stay there; you cannot do it. So Khat this argument is like many others which come from the hon. member for Lake Centre; they sound well; there is only one thing wrong with them, namely, that they will not work. And that is one which will not work. For a man to be a successful farmer he must have something which cannot be instilled into him as knowledge is acquired in a school or a law office. He must have the desire conscientiously to do his duty, and he must like
the duty he has to do. He must have a special instinct to do the job if he is to make a success of farming. Those who lack it are the ones, not infrequently, who have auction sales, leave their farms and go to the city to earn their measly $7 a day. They think they are making money; I am satisfied they are making a mistake, but maybe they have not been efficient farmers. I believe a man can make a living in the city with much less energy and ability than are needed to achieve success on a farm. Time was when the clever son used to leave the farm and be educated as a lawyer, but to-day you must have men of ability to make farming pay, and those are the only ones who are worth while keeping on the farms. Those who make a success are the ones who have the determination and the ability to do that specific work. You cannot compel people who have once acquired a taste for the glamour and bright lights of the city, to return and make a living in the country. The attractions of the city are the reason why many boys leave the farms; and remember, if it were not for the blood transfusions from the land into the cities, the standard of ability there would not be maintained for very many generations.

Will the hon. member
permit a question? He has spoken about its being necessary for a man to have an instinct for farming. Does he not think that if a farmer had a decent return for his labour, he would find the farm just as glamorous a place as the city? Would he not be satisfied if he had adequate equipment and the things he needs to make farming a decent way of living?

Some would and some would
not.

It is very easy to ask a question, but it takes a long time to give an answer to some questions, and this is one of them. I think the answer depends upon your philosophy of life and the importance you attach to certain things. I will be frank; I do not believe that the monetary return is the only reward worth while. The best things of life are the things which money cannot buy. That is not the answer the hon. member wants; but let me add this, that if you were to offer many farmers-I will not say all-the same wage to stay on the farms as they could get in the cities, they would still go to the cities. On the other hand, there are those who have a longer and broader view of the matter. If you are to try to put farming on a financial level with other industries, I concede that my arguments will not carry weight, because it just cannot be done. Many farmers keep up
Supply-Agriculture

their homes and gardens and obtain from their farms an income which goes a long way to sustain them satisfactorily, and they get many pleasures there which it is impossible to get in the city. If one appreciates these finer and better things of life, an efficient farmer on good land has an advantage over the average city man.
I would suggest to the hon. member that she might do what I did on one occasion. I asked some lawyers who are members of this house, particularly those with a clientele that is part urban and part rural, when they came to investigate the estates of these urban and rural clients who, after accumulating some property, had departed this life, which class on the whole had the most to leave. Invariably the reply I received was, "Without doubt the average farmer has more to leave after his life's effort than the average man in the city."
He takes more with him, too.

I believe there is something in that. I suppose the hon. member is thinking of the test, "What shall it profit a man if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?"
Recently I received a letter from a gentleman at Calgary who asked how much it would be necessary for a farmer and for a city man to have in order that, at the age of sixty, they could live retired in like circumstances? I took the view that if the farmer had a good 100-acre farm in Ontario, especially in the valley of Grand river, and had a life insurance of $5,000, to which he surely should have been able to add savings of another $5,000, by continuing to live on the farm he would be just as well off as the average man in the city with the income from a capital of seventy-five or eighty thousand dollars. And even at that, I think I would prefer to take a chance on the farmer living a fuller life and spending the rest of his time more happily than if he had that income in the city.
It seems to me, therefore, that to reduce this matter to calculations of dollars and cents is beside the question, because, as I have pointed out, there are other things which are valuable, for which humanity yearns, and which the farmer very often has. Not that I am trying to make out that there is no room for improvement. I hope in the post-war period consideration will be given to plans which will enable the farmers to enjoy certain standards and satisfactions of living which others enjoy, but I also believe that the duty of securing these will devolve largely upon the farmer himself.
Many things could be done in this direction. Take the matter of farm loans. The average rate of interest to-day is three per

cent. Why should the farmer be required to pay five per cent? There are many unproductive farms which will never be in a position to provide that standard of living to which the farmers are entitled, and that is a problem we shall have to face in the future. As regards man-power at the present time, the only suggestion I have to offer the Minister of Agriculture is that, so far as those 'boys are concerned who have had their basic training and therefore have a military background, they will be available if the crisis comes, and consequently it would be wise to give some of them an opportunity to volunteer to return to the land in order to help production. I say that because, if weather conditions are not favourable, we may be faced with some difficulties, and I .suggest that- if we are to invade Europe we must be prepared to feed not only our own men but the population of the places we invade. After all, food production will be a great weapon. I urge the minister to give this his best consideration. I fancy he will tell me that it is something that should be referred to the Minister of Labour. That is the only solution I have to offer, and I trust that in this debate other farmers will tell us what, in their opinion, the solution is; that they will base their proposals upon conditions as they exist instead of upon any ulterior motive., and that they will not repeat the things we have heard time and1 again, apparently for no other purpose than to gratify perhaps some of their own political ambitions. This is too serious a time for us to indulge in that sort of thing.

There is no gentleman in this house to whom I listen with, greater interest than, I do to my hon. friend who comes from the adjoining county along the banks of the Grand river, which he described a short time ago as a fertile and wonderful area. It is always a pleasure to listen to the hon. member, although sometimes I rather feel sorry for him, as I have felt to-night. He seems to have been torn between two desires. On the one hand, he would like, as he showed in his closing remarks, to convey to the government and to the committee the fact that agriculture throughout Canada, and particularly in our own district, is not in tfle happy position which, earlier in his address, he rather intimated that it held; on the other hand, he seemed to try to excuse the government for everything that has been done or that has not been done as well as for the position in which agriculture finds itself. In other W'ords, he seems to be trying to ride two horses, and between the two he has not done as well as he usually does in

Supply-Agriculture
presenting his arguments to the committee. He seemed to take particular interest in discussing something said by the hon. member for Lake Centre, and he accused that hon. gentleman of repeating arguments that had been advanced from time to time and of making suggestions that had been heard before.
I am strongly of the opinion that if more members would take the same attitude as the member for Lake Centre, repeat these arguments, and force them upon the attention of the government, we would have more accomplished than we have had in the past. The hon. member seemed to find some fault with the idea of compulsion. We have had compulsion for some time throughout Canada in connection with the man-power policy. The idea of drafting men into the army is not a new one; it has been in force for some time. I understand, moreover, that the hon. gentleman supported that policy all down the line, but before he sat down he said that it might be wise for the government to allow some of these men to return to the farm. In my opinion, in some instances at least, they should never have left the farms. He said that a good many farmers' boys want to do their share. They all do, and I fully agree with him in that regard; but I believe that a better system would have been followed if, immediately after registration had taken place in 1940-and I have said this before-each man in Canada of military age had been placed in his proper category and boys on the farms better qualified for farming had been asked or even compelled to stay there. After all, food production is just as necessary as it is for the boys to be in uniform; and if they had been compelled to stay on the farm, our food production and man-power situation, so far as the farms are concerned, would have been better to-day. At the same time,' they should have had something to show, by way of a badge or button or something of that sort, that they were doing war work just as the boys in the army are doing.
I am of the opinion that at the present time, as there has been, there is a real labour shortage throughout Canada and particularly in Ontario and in that area which the hon. member for Brant and I represent. The minister said this afternoon that a survey had been made of farms throughout the dominion. I happened to be looking that up this afternoon. There was a survey in my county of the man-power situation. There were 1,207 farmers who made returns, or from 65 to 70 per cent of those who were asked to do so. Of these 1,207 farms the average size was 122 acres. The number of male adults on^each of these farms
was 1-2; or in other words, there were twelve men of adult age on every ten farms; and the average age of these men was fifty-one years, which means that there were a considerable number of men over sixty and a good many over seventy. So that no one, even the hon. member for Brant, will deny that this is insufficient help on farms of that size, where intensive farming is carried on in dairying and the raising of live stock. It is insufficient help on any farm. I think everyone will agree with that.
Did the report give the acreage under crop, as did the survey in other counties?
Yes, I think it did.
Can the hon. member give it?

It would take some time to look it up, but it does not make much difference to my argument. These are farms that are well cultivated, where intensive farming is carried on. Not only do they raise spring grain and fall wheat and hay and clover, but they produce milk, hogs, beef cattle and pretty nearly everything else that is produced on the average Ontario farm, so far as they are able. I find that women help on 65 per cent, of these farms, which is a large average. A comment made in the report was to this effect. One farmer said that any woman who looks after a house and four children is doing her share without helping on the farm, and that is quite true.
This season some attempt has been made to overcome the difficulty, and some things have been done to try to assist the farmer to get more help. The hon. member for Lake Centre mentioned what was done on May 4, which is after all, a species of compulsion. Men are to be asked to leave certain industries and go out on the farms. Unfortunately a great many of these men are not experienced. I ran across an article which appeared in one of the morning papers which I should like to quote because it expresses my own ideas on this question. It is as follows:
Courting a Food Crisis
Simply dumping some unskilled labour on the farmer's doorstep during the rush of spring seeding will not solve the critical food problem facing us this year. As repeatedly pointed out by the Financial Post, farming is an industry in which trained labour is essential, more essential in fact than in most other industries, because agricultural workers largely operate alone and there is little opportunity for skilled supervision. Particularly is this true in the present emergency, with most farms desperately undermanned.
So far, however, the labour department at Ottawa has given not the slightest indication
Supply-Agriculture

that it has any real understanding of the problem. Not until a few months ago was any attempt made to check the drafting of skilled farm workers into the army. By then it was too late to save literally thousands of farms from going out of real production this year.
May I pause there to say that only yesterday I received a letter from a farmer in my district who stated that on account of the unfortunate wet conditions that prevail, combined with the shortage of labour, there were half a dozen farmers in his neighborhood who did not intend to sow one bit of grain this year. They were going to summer-fallow and have the land ready for next year. This does not augur very well for increased production. This article continues:
And now, when "hired men" are practically non-existent, Ottawa makes a belated move to comb workers of military age and category out of non-essential industry and force them into farm work. Most of such men, of course, will hardly be able to distinguish between a pig and and a sheep, let alone mangels from turnips or oats from barley. Furthermore, as the authorities now realize from the first call, there is only a handful of able-bodied men left in non-essential industry anyway.
I do not think it is so bad that they could not tell one animal from another, but there is no doubt that inexperienced help on a farm is of very little value. One experienced man is sometimes worth two or three others who have not had the same experience and who would be unable to carry on to the same extent.
The minister quoted figures this afternoon which seemed to prove quite conclusively that there is an urgent need for additional help on the farm. He compared the figures for 1939 with those for 1943, and they showed that there has been a falling off of adults on the farm amounting to twenty-eight per cent, while the number of hired men fell off over fifty per cent. That is conclusive evidence that there is a real shortage. That dropping off has been progressive from year to year, and I have no doubt that this year the condition will be still worse.
I did not rise to find fault or to criticize. I believe there is a real emergency at this time. I understand the minister attended the conference last fall when the different committees met and asked for increased agricultural production. I quoted some of these figures in my speech on the address in repy to the speech from the throne in order to show the increases that were being asked for. Unless something is done very soon, despite what the minister said the other day that he still felt that production would be maintained, I feel that by the end of the year, instead of an increase there will be a shortage which will be serious indeed

at this time of crisis when food is needed so badly by our armed forces and the British people.

The hon. member for
Haldimand and the hon. member for Brant have covered part of the ground fairly well. The previous speaker made a plea to tlje Minister of Agriculture. At the conclusion of his remarks the hon. member for Haldimand referred to the figures given this afternoon by the Minister of Agriculture. These figures were quite interesting; but if they are dissected they show a serious situation with respect to man-power on the farm, not only in western Canada but throughout the whole country. The figures show that as compared with 1939 there are to-day 395,000 less workers on the farm. There are only 1,778 placements in April of this year. The figures for unfilled orders were quite startling. I think the figure for Saskatchewan was 462

When we consider that
there are over 100,000 farms in Saskatchewan, we must realize that this is a very serious situation. Those of us who come from the west know there is hardly a farmer there who would refuse to take a man if he could get him at a reasonable wage. Wages in industry have increased to such an extent that farm wages have been forced up to a point where the farmer cannot compete for his labour.

The figure I quoted
a moment ago referred to unfilled orders. The total number of placements for Saskatchewan for March was 115 males and 15 females; for April, 298 males and 16 females.

I did not quote the placements; I took the unfilled orders. The total for all Canada is 1,778 placements as against 4,251 unfilled orders. As I was saying, the farmer cannot compete with prices paid to industrial labour. The minister and the government should consider instituting some control over the prices of labour and the prices of farm products. We are dealing more particularly with farm products to-night. There is not a farmer in the west who would not be willing to pay a fair wage to his labour, provided he was getting fair prices for his products. I have had some little experience of this in connection with the farms in which I am interested. When I was at home at Easter I found that wages had gone up to as high as SS5 a month. It is not that the farmers are unwilling to pay this rate; they just cannot get the men. You cannot put every Tom, Dick and Harry on a tractor,

Supply-Agriculture
especially when you are working at night. You must have a man who is reasonably experienced, because you cannot risk possible injuries to your machinery. As I say, wages are high, and there should be some way of controlling not only the cost of labour but also the prices paid for these commodities.
This afternoon the minister dealt with the programme he has asked the farmers of the west to carry out in reducing the acreage seeded to wheat this year, and he said he expected a twenty per cent decrease in that acreage. He also made the statement that the farmers will get their seed in and that, as a matter of fact, reports from the west indicate that the seeding of wheat is practically concluded and that the seeding of coarse grains is well on the way. To substantiate his argument the minister made a comparison between conditions in Canada and those in the United States and Britain, and quoted from the Saturday Evening Post of January 30, 1943, to show that conditions in Canada were as favourable as those in the United States. I should like to quote one or two press reports having to do with the same matter, but before doing so I wish to say that perhaps the programme announced by the minister in regard to decreasing the acreage seeded to wheat was not well considered before it was announced. I think in many cases the farmers will achieve the objective the minister has set, but I do not think it was a fair thing he asked them to do. The other day the Minister of Trade and Commerce gave the house figures which showed that for the 1943 crop practically the same quota per acre would be taken, with the same objective in mind, namely 280,000,000 bushels. I have in my hand a press report from Washington under date of May 14, 1943, which reads:
Anticipating that U.S. will be called on to ship large quantities of wheat to Europe in 1944, war food administrator Davis plans to ask farmers for a sharp increase in winter acreages sown next fall, and hopes to be able to get supplementary supplies from Canada and Australia.
No specific goal has been set as yet, but agriculture department grain experts said they expected Davis to ask for an increase of at least 25 per cent above this year's low level of 52,000,000 acres.
There was no indication of how much grain Davis expected to obtain from Canadian and Australian sources.
That is the situation in the United States; they are asking their producers for a twenty-five per cent increase in the acreage seeded, and they expect to make large shipments to Europe. Surely the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce
should have known about that situation, just as the authorities in the United States knew about it.
Of course that is winter wheat, to be seeded next fall.

Yes, and it will come into competition with the wheat we shall be harvesting next summer. It will be off before our harvest is over, and they even go on and say they expect to take considerable wheat from Canada. It may very well be that this year we shall need more wheat than the farmers will produce.
What I am going to say now may be a little out of order, but considerable latitude has been allowed this evening and hon. members have been permitted to speak on almost anything. In my opinion, if the farmers had been encouraged to keep the wheat in storage on their farms and increase their seeding this year, or at least seed as much as they did last year, they would have been much better off, while the labour situation would be no worse and probably not as bad as it is now. I have had some little experience in diversified farming, and I know that to produce the dairy products, meat products and coarse grains for which the minister has asked, a good deal more labour will be required than would be needed to produce the same amount of wheat that was produced last year.
The hon. member for Brant made a statement in regard to farm conditions, and I think he was right. There is no better place for a man over sixty years of age to spend the remaining years of his life than in a comfortable farm home which has all modem conveniences. If anything can be done to raise the standard of farm life at the present time, it should be done. Then, when the men come back from overseas, after having enjoyed the pleasures of the bright lights which were mentioned by the hon. member, they will be ready to settle down on good, comfortable farmsteads where, if they know their business, they may enjoy the finest and happiest life in t'he world. It is, however, important for us to see to it that farm conditions are such that there will be an improvement in the standard of life, so that when the war is over, agriculture may be able to absorb many of the young men who 'come back, for I do not think any industry in this country will be called upon to do more in that connection. I am sure the farmer has done his part in the last three years. He has done practically everything the Minister of Agriculture has asked of him, and he is willing to continue doing it. The situation

Supply-Agriculture

has become so serious, however, that this may not be possible. Many men have left the farm and gone into the army. Perhaps two or three boys may have gone from one farm, and there is only the old1 man left to carry on the work. I receive letter after letter telling me about cases of this kind. When I was at home I spoke to two or three farmers -not from my district, I am glad to say, but from the immediate vicinity-who said they could not carry on because they were not physically fit. The doctor had told them they should not do the kind of work they were doing, and unless they were given some relief they would have to leave the farm. They were going to try to get in this crop as best they could, but they said they would not undertake it another year. Therefore I say that the man-power situation, so far as agriculture is concerned, must be rectified at once.
I was going to say a word with respect to postponements, since I have had quite a little correspondence with various people in this connection, and it has been very difficult to get any satisfaction. These matters should be dealt with more speedily. I have one case in my office now which I have been taking up with the authorities for the past four weeks, without success. Something should be done along that line. Then the hon. member for Brant went on to criticize some of the statements made by hon. members on this side, and referred particularly to the hon. member for Lake Centre. I want to tell the hon. gentleman that so far as the hon. member for Lake Centre and all other hon. members of the official opposition are concerned, we have been endeavouring to offer only constructive suggestions. That is what we are here to do, and it is our duty to do it. I do not think we have been unreasonable. If we have any suggestions to make as to how the minister might straighten out his department a little, and put it in better shape, then in my opinion those suggestions should be received in the spirit in which they are given. We should not be subjected to the criticism made by the hon. member.
I failed to hear the suggestions.

There have been so
many of them; no doubt the hon. member has not been around very much of the time, because certainly there have been many suggestions. We have been criticized for making so many. If the hon. member will pay a little more attention to the business of the house, and not so much to the business of the farm, he may know more about what is going on. I know he
IMr. Perley.]
comes from a very beautiful part of the country, and I am not a bit surprised that he enjoys his week-ends at home. I have had the privilege of driving down the Grand valley, especially when it was represented by a predecessor of the hon. member. On many occasions I enjoyed myself among the beautiful scenery of Brant county and going over the splendid farming country of that constituency. So that if the hon. member was not here to listen to all the suggestions that we made, it may be on account of the very beautiful section in which he lives.
The minister, however, has been here most of the time, and I am sure he appreciates suggestions coming from this side of the house. I am pleased to say that the public generally think some of our suggestions have been the means of checking up the government. We have brought about action in not only one but many departments of government, so far as Canada's war effort is concerned. This is only one of the departments affected. In the right spirit we have offered the suggestion that the minister straighten up this matter, so that the farmers may take advantage of the situation when the time arrives.
I note that in the item for departmental administration there is an increase of $4,848, most af which is accounted for by cost of living bonuses. At the proper time I intend to say something on the point. But may I say now that when we are considering the cost of living bonus we must remember that the farmer is paying an increased price for foods and accommodation, and some consideration might be given to permitting cost of living bonus to farm labour, so that they may be placed on a par with civil servants. I believe most of the increase I have indicated will go as cost of living bonus to members of the civil service, if I understand correctly the details appearing at page 53 of the estimates.

May I at this point
express my profound respect for the farmer. The son of a farmer, myself, I have always found farmers intelligent, whether they were Progressive Conservatives or reform Liberals. That makes very little difference. They are honest. As I listened to the hon. member for Haldimand and the hon. member for Brant, my belief was confirmed. My first impression of farmers was that they could discuss a question intelligently, whether that question was the old one of predestination or free grace, or whether it

Supply-Agriculture
was a discussion as to how to obtain the best production by the rotation of crops. The subject	matter	made	very little
difference.
I listened to these hon. members tonight, and I am sure the Minister of Agriculture listened to them. They displayed practical common sense. I have only one suggestion to make: I would count it a great honour if the Minister of Labour or the Minister of Agriculture would allow me to present a list of the names qf young men who had to leave the farms, but who wanted to stay there and would be extremely glad to go back. I would give that list to the Minister of Labour or to the deputy minister. I believe these young men could give far better service to their country if they -were on the farms than they can give in training centres.
One farmer at the head of the lakes told me that some of our farmers in that district had made a mistake in going into aeroplane factories, or engaging in other war work. He said that his three boys had gone into the air force; that his daughter was a culinary expert, and that he was better off to-day, financially, than he had ever been on the farm. That man is nearly seventy years of age. He is taking a man's place on the farm, and is producing more than ever.
I join with hon. members in saying that the farmer need not take second place to anybody in Canada, so far as engaging in an all-out war effort is concerned. However, I believe that as a result of the desire of registrars to swell the armed forces some young men have been taken unjustly. They should have an opportunity of returning to the farms, and I shall be glad in a short time to give a list of young men who would be eligible for such transfer.

The item for administration
in the estimates is of a general nature, and permits of general discussion. I crave indulgence of the committee to say a few words respecting two or three matters which come to my attention.
When the hon. member for Qu'Appelle has occasion to advance suggestions in the committee, he always puts forth the plea that things should be done differently. Well, probably they should. As I understood his remarks to-night, he was inclined to be critical of the government's action with respect to encouraging the curtailment of wheat production in western Canada, In that sense I think we should look at the situation as a whole on the north American continent. I happen to have before me a booklet entitled
Canadian Coarse Grains Quarterly Review", and shall refer to only one or two passages. It states:
Despite all this drawing on Canadian supplies, however, and the efforts of United States farmers to meet the goals set for war crops, the latest survey of the United States feed situation, based on crop prospects for 1943, suggests that the supply of feed grains per grain-consuming animal in 1943-44 will be 10 to 15 per cent below the supply in 1942-43. This calculation takes into account the wheat and rye supply that might be diverted to animal feeding.
Later on, it says:
Live stock production in the United States is now at record levels and further increases are expected this year. Altogether it is estimated that the units or numbers of grainconsuming animals for the calendar year 1943 will be 10 to 12 per cent above the number recorded for the calendar year 1942. This heavy growth in live stock population promises to cut deeply into feed stocks in the crop year 1943-44.
Having those two statements in mind, I am bound to say I believe it will be generally recognized that the government's policy, urging a reduction in the production of wheat and an increase in the production of coarse grains, has been a sound one. And as time goes on, probably before the end of this year and certainly before the end of next, it will be so proven. In fact, I venture the observation that unless at least normal crops of coarse grains are produced in Canada and the United States this coming year, we may find ourselves in a short position, so far as feed grains are concerned. That being so, I submit it is reasonable to say that the policy of the government urging the reduction in wheat supplies for the time being, together with getting the land into an improved condition to grow wheat when there is an opportunity to market it, and turning that production where possible into the production of coarse grains, through which live stock and live stock products, so essential in the war effort, can be stimulated, was a sound policy to follow, and will be so proven.
The discussion to-night hinges largely round the question of man-power, so far as agriculture is concerned. I do not think we should go to extremes on either side. There is no one in the house who will not admit that there is a tight position as regards man-power on the farm. Moreover, there is no one who understands the farming industry who will not agree that it requires a different type of labour from that needed in other industries. On the farm one cannot give the same type of supervision and the detailed special training in preparing a man to carry on operations on the land that can be given in other industries.
Supply-Agriculture

Therefore the farmer, if he is to produce efficiently, must have an efficient, experienced man, and that is where the chief difficulty arises at the present time. But even recognizing that to be the situation, I remind the committee that last year the farmers of Canada produced and harvested the biggest crop ever harvested in the dominion, with the man-power they had at that time. The farmers of this country are resourceful, and when forced to it can make all kinds of short-cuts to accomplish what is asked of them. They did so last year; they are doing so now, and I hope they will continue to do so.
Was not that due to the fact that most of the harvesting was done with combines, requiring little labour, rather than with the binder and thresher?

I was just coming to that point in a slightly different way. It is quite true that combines were used in large sections of Canada. I hope that will be the situation this year, that the crop will be harvested by the same combines, although now a little more worn out.
What I was about to say was this: My observations lead me to believe that the farmers to-day are cooperating with one another and utilizing one another's machinery to a greater extent than they probably ever did before. They get their neighbours to do a job that they cannot do, and in every way possible they are attempting to meet the problems they have to face at a given season.
Another factor which affects the farm labour situation and the prospects of putting in and harvesting the crop to a substantial degree and which is recognized by anyone with experiences on the farm is seasonal conditions. I have heard many Ontario farmer friends complain bitterly this spring on account of the difficulties in certain sections of Ontario owing to wet weather which has delayed the putting in of the crop. That is a hazard the farmer has to face. If a wet season develops in spring or at harvest time, it is a serious matter for the farmer. That is a particular feature of the farm labour situation, because a large part of the crop may be damaged at harvest time if there is not a pool of man-power upon which to draw to take care of it.
There has been some comment on the figures given by the minister regarding applications made to employment agencies throughout Canada and the number of applications that were filled for farm employment. The figures were rather difficult for me to understand. I submit, however, that the farmers by and large do not use employment agencies. That may be a mistake. Moreover, I am going to suggest, if I may, that in many

instances the farmers have not been any too fair to these employment agencies. They have sent for a man, and perhaps not having their order filled by the employment agency for a week or two, they have in the meantime hired another man who happened to come along, so that when a man was sent out by the employment agency they did not want him. The fair thing to do, of course, would be to notify the employment agency that help had been secured. I doubt very much if the experienced farm labourer ayails himself bf the employment agencies. He knows the people he has worked for before and the districts he likes to go to, and in a general way he knows where there is likely to be employment. Moreover, everyone knows that temperament and personality enter into the [DOT] question of farm employment to a very great degree. A farmer would much prefer to have a man with whom he was acquainted from the point of view of temperament, disposition and his willingness to work than take a chance on hiring someone whom he did not know, and the same applies to the man who is looking for a job. Therefore the explanation with regard to farm placement rests largely on that fact, that both the farmer and the labourer have made their own arrangements without going to the employment agencies.
One would be inclined to think that this matter had not been faced up to so far as government is concerned. But I happen to know that in Manitoba efforts have been made in a definite way to meet the farm labour situation with as practical an approach as can be made under the circumstances. All recognize that there is a tight farm labour situation. I think we all realize as well that there is a strained situation with respect to labour in every form of industry or business. I was talking not long ago to a friend in Winnipeg who is in the laundry business, and he told me that he had to increase his staff about one-third in order to take care of the same amount of business he did previously, simply because he could not get experienced help. Go into the restaurants or any other business, and you will find that they are all having difficulty in securing trained, efficient labour. In the carrying on of a war the situation could not be otherwise. If it were otherwise, there would be complaints that the full effort of the country was not being put forward in the prosecution of the war.
I have under my hand a little statement sent me by a municipality in my part of the country. It is a report on production meetings held in that municipality. The first meeting I presume was called to discuss the production objectives that were outlined by the Minister

Supply-Agriculture
of Agriculture last December and were mentioned in the house early this session. I wish to refer to two or three features of this report.
In the first place it says that in this particular municipality five meetings were held at which there was an average attendance of twenty-eight farmers. The first meeting was held on March 26. The reeve, the secretary-treasurer, the agricultural representatives of the government and the councillors organized the meetings, and the first meeting was addressed' by Mr. Richmond of the Manitoba pool elevator staff, by Mr. Foster, of the extension service, and by Mr. Johnson, agricultural representative of the Manitoba Department of Agriculture. A general discussion followed the presentation of the needs for increased production of food supplies, and committees were set up to organize the outlying section of the municipality with the object of bringing to the attention of the people the production goals so that they could be organized to achieve the goals set. The reeve and the councillors were asked to do the organizing. They arranged for meetings to be held in different parts of the municipality. The report goes on to say that the discussions at these meetings were very encouraging, and here is a special reference to the farm labour problem:
Practically every farmer is short of help. Most farmers feel that they cannot afford to pay the wages asked particularly for inexperienced help. Unless a hired man has had some experience and is dependable he would be a liability rather than an asset on the average farm. The problem of a seasonable supply of labour on the majority of farms does not exist as it did a few years ago. Most farmers keep a considerable quantity of live stock and help is needed every day of the year. Power machinery and the use of combines has materially lessened the need of extra help at harvest time. There is however a need of extra help ... in haying time. . . .
The point I wish to make here particularly is that these people set out an estimate-I will not take the time to read it-that they would require fifty or sixty men in the community to take care of haying operations, and that these men could then probably be transferred to the harvesting operations; but they do not make any reference to a shortage of man-power to put in the present crop. From my own observation I would say that for the most part, while the farmers have not in all instances efficient help, nor in all instances as much help as they would like to have, most of them are going to get by, as far as putting the crop in is concerned, in the immediate district where I have had an opportunity to make any observations. The difficulty is more likely to arise later on.
I should like, however, to come back to what is already under way in Manitoba. A few nights before I returned east I listened to a broadcast made by the deputy minister of agriculture of that province wherein he outlined the agreement which had been entered into with the federal government, and went on to indicate the steps which had been taken by a committee set up in Manitoba to deal particularly with farm labour requirements. He assured the farmers that as far as possible an attempt would be made to meet their needs, and he went on to say that they were trying to provide for the utilization of a number of people of different classes. I believe he mentioned, that the services of older people and young people would be called upon, that they hoped they might be abje to utilize to some extent the labour of Japanese, Indians, conscientious objectors and maybe prisoners of war, and that there was a prospect of the odd internee being available. So that the problem is being attacked, and I believe that with the cooperation of the farmers, and of the business men who may have to give some attention to this matter, an honest attempt will be made to meet requirements.
However, in the report which was forwarded to me, these people go on to say that more encouragement should be given to farm' boys to remain on the farm rather than enlist in the armed services, and that more consideration should be given to the farm boys now in the services for seeding and harvesting leaves. They go as far as to suggest that railway fares on these leaves should be reduced to the minimum. Perhaps they have got a point there worthy of consideration, and I support the suggestion of the hon.. member for Brant in that regard. It seems to me that these people who are in training camps could be made available to a greater extent, certainly for seasonal employment. If steps to that end can be taken, I hope they will be, because that would relieve the situation to a substantial degree.
The same people make a further observation, one which was mentioned the other evening by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle and the hon. member for Melfort, namely, that farm wages are out of line with industrial wages and that a .bonus should be paid in some form to farm labourers. While I have sympathy with the suggestion, I wish the hon. gentlemen who raised it would sugr gest some means whereby a bonusing scheme could be made applicable to the farm labour situation, particularly as it applies in western Canada; or there might be a set wage, if you like. I believe that a set wage would
Supply-Agriculture

immediately become the general wage, and that you would have in turn bonuses or other concessions being paid which were not recorded at the time. Moreover, you would have the less efficient claiming the same wage as a set wage, and the bonus as well. I am bound1 to say that so far as this particular matter is concerned1 I think it should be approached from the other angle. If the farmer cannot pay the wage rate available to industry and whereby he may keep a man working for him, it is the farmer's problem rather than the farm labourer's problem, and should be attacked accordingly. In other words, the farmer should be provided with an income whereby he can pay the wage, instead of an attempt being made to work out the details of a plan to apply a' bonus system to farm labour.
But here, again, I wish to refer to a matter which I discussed earlier; and I hope that for the moment, Mr. Chairman, you will not rule me out of order. We have income tax exemptions applying to amounts lower than $660 and $1,200. If farmers are checked carefully and are obliged to make an income tax return, I venture to say that more will be paying income tax than are doing so at the present time; and if that is so, the bonus to the labourer which he could not show as a deduction from his farm income might place him more readily in the income tax brackets than he otherwise would be, so that I am not sure that even that is the answer. But my hon. friends point out that labour in industry and government civil servants are securing a cost of living bonus, some of it paid by the state-which is true. Yet I must remind my hon. friends that agriculture at the present time is not totally overlooked in this regard. I have before me a little statement, which I had prepared, indicating that bonuses, direct and indirect, to the farmers of Canada-all of Canada- since 1939 have amounted to $142,000,000. I contend that it is fair to argue that assistance indirectly paid in this manner can foe looked upon in some degree at least as a cost of living bonus paid to the farmer; and out of that he must of necessity, where he has to engage labour, recognize his position in that respect.
That is the total amount, is it?
That is the total amount for all Canada, including fertilizer bonuses.
For one year?

No; since 1939.
Mr.DOUGLAS (Weyburn): Roughly, about $150 per capita?
Most of it was in the last three years.
Has the hon. member figured out what that amounts to per capita?

My hon. friend is better at arithmetic than I am; I will leave him to work it out.
I mention these matters merely to indicate that the farmer's position has not been overlooked. Moreover, I believe the farmer recognizes his position at the present time and is prepared to produce to the limit of his capacity. '
The one person in the farm picture for whom I have a little more sympathy than for anyone else, and whose position has not been mentioned here to-night, is the farm wife. The problem of securing domestic assistance where needed-and in some places it is needed badly -I am bound to say is much more critical than even the problem of outside labour.
It is not part of the hon. member's problem.
How would the hon. member know?

Well, sometimes we have experiences which are not obvious on the surface.
Before I resume my seat I would point out to the minister that this problem of farm labour is one which requires constant attention, and that if he can use his influence in any degree with the rest of his cabinet colleagues to secure the seasonal help of at least some of those now in the armed forces, to assist in taking off the crop, particularly if the season becomes bad, it will materially benefit farm production.

The hon. member who has just spoken brought forward some of the suggestions I intended to make on this particular item. The fact that the government has failed to take any practical farmer into consultation in its deliberations and to get advice and suggestions from him has been the basis of most of the mistakes that have been made. Some hon. members opposite would like to leave the impression that no mistakes have been made, that everything is perfectly fine in this best of all possible worlds. There is no use in putting our heads in the sand and saying that a problem does not exist. It does exist, and it is a very pressing problem. One of the chief causes of the trouble is the fact which everyone recognizes, that labour is scarce. That is only natural in war time, but what the farmer does not like is the fact that the available labour is inequitably distributed.

I know personally farmers who have been compelled to quit farming because labour has been taken from them. This is general in many parts of Saskatchewan at any rate. For the past five months-last fall and this spring -farmers have been selling out by the dozen. I know cf one district, an area within seven miles of one point, where twenty farmers on good land have sold out lock, stock and barrel and gone out of the province. That has been a common thing in Saskatchewan during the past six months. The trouble is that one farmer finds, when his last son has been taken from him, that across the road there is another farmer on a smaller piece of land, with less production, where there are still two or three sons. That is the galling thing. It is the injustice that exasperates him and convinces him that there is no equitable policy upon which he may rely.
The government has failed to carry out a definite policy with regard to man-power, and that is the basis of most of the trouble. The farmer is willing to accept his share of the burden. He has proven himself both in times of peace and during the war. He has shown that he will take his place among the citizens of Canada in meeting, any emergency. He will sacrifice with any of them. He has shown his position over and over again. In the production of grain what do we find? I believe the farmer is away ahead of the government's policy in the production of wheat. The farmers infer from the policy of the government that it does not want his wheat; that it wants to discourage the growing of grain. The day is not far distant, however, when the world will require all the grain and wheat it can get.
We are not discouraging the production of grain.
You are discouraging the production of grain at the present time.
No.
You are paying a bonus for wheat reduction.
We are paying a bonus for the production of other grains rather than wheat, but not for a reduction in grains.
You are not encouraging the growing of grain when the farmer is left in the west with a billion bushels of it, half of which he cannot sell.
He must have grown quite a bit. when he has a billion bushels lying there.

He has a billion bushels
on the farms in the west to-day.
Which does not indicate that we have been discouraging the growing of grain. We are encouraging it.

You are discouraging it when you make it impossible for the farmer to sell it. That is why he is going out; he cannot sell his product. He is told that there are quotas in the elevators, and when he tries to deliver he is told, "there is no room here."
Is he not feeding more live stock?

Yes, but that takes more labour. He is asked to turn what grain he has into meat and dairy products, but that requires more labour and he is finding it more difficult to get labour. There are 395,000 men taken out of agriculture, and the farmer is asked to produce more. Anyone who knows anything about the subject knows it takes a good deal of work to turn that grain, after producing it, into the finished meat product. Before he can do that he must have some knowledge of what the future holds for him. If he is to go into the production of meat, he must have some assurance that labour will be available on the farm for two or three years, because you cannot produce a herd of cattle, whether dairy or beef cattle, in one season. But the farmer has no guarantee, at least he has not had a guarantee so far, that even if he does plan producing, the labour will be left on the farm. Then, when his boy has left the farm and he requires some labour in the fall, he finds that men are brought from other parts of Canada and he has to pay wages as high as $6 a day for harvest help. His own boy has gone and he has to pay these other young men a very high wage. Wages this spring in Saskatchewan were as high as $75, $80 and $100 a month. The farmer cannot sell his wheat; he cannot possibly pay labour the price that is demanded.
I endorse what the hon. member who preceded: me said, namely, that skilled labour on the farm is a valuable asset. Taking unskilled labour out of industry and putting it on the farm can do more harm than good, with valuable machinery in such hands. Skilled farm labour is indeed a valuable asset. A good man is worth a great deal; a poor man is a liability. If you take these men out of industry and force them to go on the farm, which apparently,is part of the labour policy, the very fact that you force them on the farms makes them dissatisfied. It will not work. The farmer will produce whatever the
Supply-Agriculture

government wants him to produce. He will do his bit if only the government will tell him exactly where he stands and what he is required to do. I believe the farmer will go on producing anything the government wants him to produce, but in my opinion the government's policy is wrong. If they are looking for greater production of food they had better revise their wheat and labour policy.
The Minister of Agriculture said that he was not responsible for the labour situation. I would say this to him. He has been a . member of the man-power committee of the cabinet continuously for the last three or four years. He was in charge of the original registration when it took place in 1940, and it has fallen on evil days.

My hon. friend does not wish to misrepresent the position. I said I was not responsible for explaining to this committee the situation in relation to labour; that is the responsibility of the Minister of Labour. I assume my responsibility along with that of every other hon. member of the government for any situation that exists in connection with labour.

I am glad the minister is willing to accept that responsibility. He sat here as a minister when the Prime Minister, in March, 1942, said that all key men in agriculture would be frozen on the farms. In spite of that, men who were key men in agriculture were called off the farms by hundreds. The national selective service board had complete power. This was only one of the mistakes they made. These boards were given no basis on which to make a selection except to say: If we think you are a key man then you will be allowed to stay on the farm. If we do not think so, then you will not. What does "key man" mean? Some point system should have been set up. For every hundred acres under cultivation, for so many cattle, so many hogs, so many heads of poultry, so many dairy cattle and so on, one able-bodied man would be left. Provided that production was maintained, then the farmer should be guaranteed that he would not be called up. The war services board took whatever information they had

I think in many cases it was incomplete-and the final result was that many farms were depleted of most valuable skilled labour.
Where do we stand with regard to the future? I should like the minister to state to-day where Canada stands with regard to the production of food at the present time and in the post-war period. We should be looking a little ahead of the immediate problem. What is Canada's position with regard to the sup-

plying of grain to the markets that are available? Most world markets are not available to us. The United States needs wheat. The visible carryover in the United States this year is probably half of what would be consumed in that country in one year. They are negotiating now to take Canadian feed wheat into their country. Where are they buying that grain? Are they buying it through the Canadian wheat board or on the open market? Is duty being paid on that wheat when it enters the United States? Who gets the advantage? Is the farmer, the man who produced the -wheat, getting his cost of production out of it? Are his interests being properly protected? I think a statement from the minister on these matters would help a great deal.
What about the hundreds of millions of bushels of wheat still on the farms of western Canada? Where does the western farmer stand with regard to this surplus wheat? Is it ever to be used? Is it of any value? These are the things the minister should be telling the farmer. The government should be laying their plans for the future so that the farmer will know where he stands?
What does the hon. member think about the matter?

I think every bushel that is out there will be needed. The government would be doing the wise thing if they paid the farmer an advance for all the grain that is properly stored on his farm. He is carrying it, and he will be carrying it until it is needed by the world. The longer this war lasts, the more this wheat will be needed.
I know farmers who are leaving their farms, who cannot sell their wheat and are leaving it in granaries on their farms. They are moving out of the district and are leaving their wheat in the bins. The government should have done sooner what is being done now in the way of calling in representative practical farmers from the municipalities in the various areas throughout the country. The problem should be put in front of them, and they should be told what was required. They should be asked their solutions of the problem. If that had been done earlier and their advice followed, we would not be running into the mess we are . now in.
There is no mess. We have received just what we asked for each year. What mess is there in that?

I believe conferences are taking place throughout the west at the present time. Each municipality has been asked to fill in a form with regard to production, man-power and the labour, problems of the area.

Supply-Agriculture
These matters have been dealt with just as soon as they needed to be dealt with.

That may be the minister's opinion, but the fact is that farmers are leaving the land; they are selling out. Some of them have been forced to leave the land. We should be doing the same thing for our farmers as we have been asking the government to do for labour, namely, to bring labour in to discuss these matters which affect labour. If that had been done, the government would be much farther ahead with their farm labour problems.
My hon. friend speaks of a mess, which is an easy term to use. Is not the statement he has just made an indication of organization, not a mess?
I think what is being done now is just a little bit late.
That is begging the question.
I think the Minister of Labour will recognize that there was a mess with regard to national selective service.
The Minister of Labour does not recognize anything-
Oh, oh.
Confession is good for the soul.
My hon. friend did not let me finish. The Minister of Labour does not recognize the mess that my hon. friend speaks about; that is all.
It is a mess, though.

I wish the Minister of Labour would come out to Saskatchewan and hear some of the complaints I have heard and see some of the farms and what some of the people are trying to do. He should go into their homes-they are most hospitable people-and see some of the problems, they are facing. I think he would recognize the truth in some of the things I have said to-night.
The hon. member's district has never been as well off in all its history.

My last suggestion to the minister is that he should make a statement with regard1 to future policies. He should tell us where Canada stands with regard to the supply of food, both for the immediate present and for the post-war period. He should advise these farmers what to do with the supplies of food that are already on hand.

Having heard a number of suggestions this evening and yesterday from farmers, both practical and armchair, I should like to say a few words by way of general discussion and then a little later on go into more detail as the different items are being discussed. I must thank the hon. member for Brant for having entertained' us again this evening. Apparently he felt much better after having had his dinner. I am sorry that he did not take the time to think through some of the suggestions and recommendations which he made.
For instance, he said that farmers are paying off their mortgages. Does the hon. member for Brant realize that the accomplices of the mortgage companies have removed all debt protective legislation and left our farmers to the mercy of the mortgage companies? In order to pay these sums of money, many farmers have been compelled to sell unfinished live stock and sacrifice other things. They have been forced to do these things in order to provide an argument for those who are against the farmer and in favour of the present set-up. He went on to tell us that in days gone by the farmer usually sent his smart son into the law profession or some such occupation. I would include in that the banking profession. I wonder why the hon. member's father changed that procedure in his case and kept his smart son on the farm.
The hon. member for Macdonald made a number of sound suggestions. I am compelled to agree with some of them, but I cannot agree with them all. He told us that the farmers had1 not been neglected altogether in the matter of bonuses. He mentioned a figure of $142,000,000 which had been paid as bonuses during the past four years, but the fact is that the farmers received only a small portion of that to which they are entitled. Further benefits were denied them by means of price freezing and restrictions on the growing of grain. If our farmers were given treatment equal to that given to labour-I am not against what is being done for labour-it would mean an extra seventy cents a bushel on the wheat grown. If the hon. member for Macdonald or any other hon. member, on that or this side of the house, wants to work out what our present set-up is costing us, just let him figure an extra seventy cents on every bushel of wheat we grow. If the farmer received this money, he would be well able to pay his mortgage debts and decent wages to his farm help.
The question of farm labour was discussed last evening, and I must say that I agree with a number of the suggestions made at that time. I hope action will be taken soon to

Supply-Agriculture

put some of the non-essential industries out of the running and move some of that help around so that other industries may have the benefit of it. However, I hope that none of those inexperienced1 people are sent to the farms. I can picture a beauty parlour operator, for example, being sent out to the farm. Probably we would find him manicuring the toenails of the cow in the morning instead of milking her. I remember some years ago when harvest excursions were run to the west; on one occasion we had1 a barber on the farm who could not be induced to set the sheaves the right way up. He had the heads down and the butts up; though he was told many times how it should be done he would not do it right, so that finally he had to be put on the road. Therefore I suggest, for the benefit of the Minister of Labour, that help of this kind be sent where it will be of more use than on the farm. So far as is humanly possible only experienced farm help Should be sent to the farmers. We all realize that at the present time, with the armed forces and war industries looking for men, we cannot send the number necessary back to the farms, but my suggestion is that as far as possible experienced farm workers now engaged in industry, and perhaps some of those in the armed services, be returned to agriculture and those workers from non-essential industries sent into the factories and perhaps the armed forces as well.
On February 26 last I read to>
the house a questionnaire that had been sent out by one of those "produce for victory" organizations in my constituency. This was in the municipal district of Wainwright which is composed of forty townships, and I should like to give some of the information gained through a survey of that territory, because I believe this would represent the average requirements of other districts in that part of the country. It was estimated that to complete threshing some 385 men would be required, while some 152 men would be required for putting in the crop this spring. I do not know where that many men could be found in that part of the country; they simply are not there. I returned from there only a very short time ago, and I feel quite satisfied that a number of farms will be run shorthanded, while much more summer-fallow will be worked this summer than would be the situation if labour were available and the crop could be disposed of after it had been grown. This committee has been operating for the past four years, and on April 10 it held its fifth annual conference. This conference works in active cooperation with provincial and dominion officials; I believe it is

very active and is doing very good work, with representatives of various interested bodies included in the membership. After the conference they sent me a number of recommendations, a few of which I am going to read. In speaking of the aims of the conference, they say:
This farm conference desires to state that we will do everything possible to maintain and increase farm production in 1943-44, recognizing that food and industrial crops are an imperative necessity towards winning the war against fascism, to build a free world and ensure a democratic peace, in which we Canadian farmers shall have an opportunity to improve our own welfare along with the peoples of the united nations.
However, we fear that production cannot be increased, and may be decreased, unless certain measures are taken by the federal and provincial governments within their respective spheres.
Then they go on with some recommendations, including the following:
Other sources of farm labour might be found in cutting advertising down, commercial travelling, and in bringing about cooperative operation of stores, and the transfer of those released to war industries, so releasing ex-farm workers to go back to the farms. We also recommend that the government pay railway fares of men in the armed forces, being released for farm work, to and from the farms.
Then they also say:
In the meantime, it is our opinion that farmers must learn to cooperate in their work more effectively.
In that connection I must say, as another hon. member has said, that farmers are working together at the present time better than I have ever seen them work together during my years in the west.
Labour saving machinery be made more readily available through the zone committees and definite guarantee of replacement of machines and repairs be given, as it has come to our attention that farmers are reluctant to do custom work unless such guarantee is assured.
Another recommendation is that small loans be made to farmers at a reasonable rate of interest; the suggestion here is three per cent.
They continue:
In our opinion, most of the farmer's financial problems and to a certain degree labour problems could be met if guaranteed prices for all essential products were paid at a rate of five per cent above cost of production and the guaranteed price maintained for not less than two years after the war ends.
Fear of the sudden curtailment of markets, for live stock in particular, is being expressed by many farmers. This is retarding expansion at the present time. In our opinion, if this fear is removed, there would be a greater readiness to expand those kinds of live stock production that do not require much labour and constant care.
