The last paragraph in the submission reads:
This conference rejects any idea of a farm strike, which would only jeopardize the cause of the united nations, but respectfully warns the governments concerned that unless greater measures of cooperation in regard to labour, finance, prices, and machinery requirements is developed between the governments and farmers, there may easily develop a grave crisis in food production in Canada.
That is signed by R. Garneau as secretary of the organization.
We have been told that we produced a large crop in 1942. I am quite ready to admit that, but I fear there is a disappointment in store for many of those who are firmly convinced that the requirements of the Minister of Agriculture will be met. I have in my hand a statement showing the average yield in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta for the twenty-three years from 1920 to 1942 inclusive. In the case of Manitoba we have an average wheat yield for that period of 16-2 bushels per acre. The high year was 26-9 bushels, in 1942, while the low year was 9 bushels per acre, in 1935. In the case of oats the average is 27-5 bushels per acre, with 47-3 bushels the high in 1942 and 16 - 7 bushels the low in 1927. In the case of barley the average is 22-4 bushels; the high year was 1942 with 36-6 bushels, while the low year was 1936, with 13-3 bushels.
Corning now to Saskatchewan, I would ask hon. members to take particular note of the yields in that province, because they are sufficient to prove that the arguments which have been made here time and again in years gone by were not unfounded. The high yield of wheat in Saskatchewan was 27-1 bushels per acre, in 1942, and the low yield was 2-6 bushels in 1937. This latter amount is just, about sufficient grain to seed an acre for two years, and it has to be pretty clean seed at that. If one takes much out there would not be sufficient left. Then, in respect of oats the high was 52 bushels per acre in 1942, and the low was 5-1 bushels in 1937. In respect to barley the high was 37-3 bushels in 1942, and) the low 4-7 bushels in 1937, with an average of 20-2 bushels in twenty-three years.
Then, coming to Alberta we find the average yield of wheat for twenty-three years was 15-9 bushels per acre, with a high of 28-0 bushels in 1923, and a low of 8-8 bushels in 1936. In the case of oats we find an average of 28-1 bushels over the period, with a high last year of 53-3 bushels and a low of 19-7
bushels in 1936. In respect of barley wre had an average of 22-4 bushels in the 23-year period, with a high of 39 bushels last year, and a low of 16-5 bushels in 1922.
Therefore, if hon. members will take the trouble to look over the yields in the past number of years, they will find that we might very easily run into a shortage of grain. And if we encounter that shortage, we are sure to have a shortage of live stock production.
One of the things that we need most at the present time is parity prices. Since I have come to the house, hon. members have argued for parity prices. We are still arguing for them, but we are not getting them. It seems that we need a leader in any line, and in this connection I will read the words of Mr. Claude R. Wickard1, who is well known to the Minister of Agriculture and other members of the government. Speaking to a senate committee not long ago he said:
During recent years, it has become clear that farmers have won their battle for recognition of parity. Farmers fought twenty years for parity. I am proud to have had a part in that fight and I intend to fight just as hard to maintain parity. Farmers have convinced the general public that parity with industrial prices is a fair and honest yardstick for measuring farm prices.
No one would be happier than I if the Minister of Agriculture were to rise in his seat to-night, make a similar statement and have the government support him. I am satisfied he is doing what he can, but it seems we have other hurdles to jump before we reach that position. I hope hon. members on all sides of the house, as well as members of the government, will see to it that in the near future agriculture is given a square deal. As I have said on other occasions, we cannot have a happy or prosperous country with one-half slave and the other half free.
There are a number of other questions I intend to discuss at the appropriate time, including live stock prices, wool prices and matters of that kind, but because I would expect other hon. members might wish to speak at this time, I shall let my position rest.

If we are to justify our existence as a deliberative assembly, we must look at some of these problems from different angles, and consider all phases. I would draw the attention of hon. members to a few things which have been done and which are being done for agriculture. I would say first of all that the quota system, in regard to the marketing of wheat, has worked out reasonably well. There are districts I have the honour to represent in which, on account of its resistance

to drought, wheat is about the only crop that can ibe profitably grown. Wheat farmers have had a pretty hard time of it. Last winter they had wheat lying out in the fields and in open bins because lumber was not available with which to build granaries. But their position would have been very much worse had they had to depend on an open market, and had they not been able to have their quota, small as it was, and to get a price for that wheat which, although less than the cost of production, was yet better than they could have obtained in any other way.
Markets have been arranged for live-stock products, including cattle, bacon and commodities of that kind. Free freight has been arranged on feeds and, as has been said, a tremendous amount of money has been paid out by way of bonuses. The bonuses on cheese, butterfat and bacon, as well as bonuses when crops have failed in some years, and where the farmer is reducing his wheat acreage, have helped a great deal.
I feel, however, that the majority of farmers in Canada, are in an inferior position, as compared with people in other lines of endeavour. I would speak particularly about irrigation farmers and ranchers. Where farming is carried on, there are periods when extra help is needed. The younger men who .have been called away are the ones who understand machinery, and who have had experience in farm work. Their services in some instances are desperately needed. Many of the older people are carrying on under physical handicaps, and are trying to do work they are unable to do.
Irrigation work is not only seasonal; the labour is required all the year round'. If the production of irrigation farms and ranches is to be kept up, some extra help must be given to these people. If we recall what the Minister of National Defence for Air said this afternoon about the heroic deeds of those who are in the forefront of this battle, we shall realize that any sacrifice we make is as nothing when compared with those they are making. At the same time, however, we must keep up our food supplies. I make this appeal, not only to the Minister of Agriculture-because he knows about it-but to other members of the cabinet, to try to readjust our prices. The prices of commodities we have to buy and of those we have to sell must be readjusted, so that the farming economy will be able to survive, and all classes will be on a more even basis.

I should like to ask a question of the minister. But before asking it, may I say that I agree with much of what was said by the hon. member for Macdonald. However, he seemed to be in a bit of a quandary as to how we were to create parity for the farmer, either by bonusing or by increasing prices.
He pointed out that since the beginning of the war this government had made available about $142,000,000 for farmers, by way of bonuses. I would point out that that amount is only about eight per cent of the amount the same government has made available in the same period for industry, by way of capital assistance. Capital assistance for industry during the same period has been made available to the extent of $1,723,827,000. So that the hon. member may figure it out for himself.
Not only that, but I pointed out before that, as a result of the steel strike last fall, ordinary labour was guaranteed fifty-five cents an hour, by order in council. From these figures one can easily see whether agriculture is getting its just share of the fruits of the war effort.
I do not wish to prolong the debate unduly, but I must say that a great deal must still be done in order to secure parity for agriculture. It has been recognized that the production of foodstuffs is just as essential as anything else in the war effort, and will probably be more essential in the post-war period.
On January 15 the minister spoke at Brandon, in respect of beef, and is quoted on January 16 as follows:
Consumption of beef and large shipments to United States, where meats could be specially prepared for overseas shipments in cans, had resulted in a possible beef shortage in the dominion, Mr. Gardiner stated, and thus permits were now required for shipments across the line.
If that is correct, I should like to know.

I do not recall saying anything about the tinning of beef, but that interpretation may have been placed on something that was said at that time. The statement I made in Brandon was this:	If the
farmers intended to have any beef go to the United States in the coming year they would have to produce sufficient to feed the Canadian people and have a surplus to send to the United States, and there was a possibility, of course, of the Americans themselves processing meat. I did not say, in cans.
But we have not done anything in that respect?

We made an announcement yesterday in regard to the present position in relation to beef. That statement was

published in the papers this morning, indicating that there will be supplies of beef in frozen form sent to Britain if there is a surplus over and above what we require in Canada for our own purposes.
But we have not been doing anything on that up to date?
There have been no shipments out of Canada up to date, because we have required for our own purposes all the beef marketed since last fall.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a remark or two with reference to the farm labour situation, which has been discussed for the greater part of the evening. I agree with the minister when he says that the discussion of the man-power problem generally comes within the purview of the Minister of Labour and personally I shall be very glad to leave the discussion of that problem until the Minister of Labour is discussing the matter under the war appropriation bill.
But there is one fact of which the committee ought not to lose sight, namely, that the Minister of Agriculture is on the man-power committee of the cabinet, it seems to me, for one specific reason, and that is to guarantee to agriculture what he considers to be a sufficient supply of man-power to enable agriculture to fulfil its commitments both with reference to Canada itself and to the united nations. We cannot discuss to-night the whole question of man-power. It appears to me that there the lack has been a master plan to allocate manpower. I know it is not an easy thing to do. For a long time we had different departments of govemmeht competing one with another for the services of the same man. One department was asking men to come into the army, another into the air force, another into the navy, another into munitions factories, and still another department was urging the men to stay on the farm and produce. We are in the course now, under national selective service, of doing some of the things that should have been done a long time ago, and it is always more difficult to go back than to meet the situation when the problem first arises.
When the hon. member for Brant said to-night that the hon. member for Lake Centre did not know w'hat he was talking about-the hon. member for Lake Centre does not need me to defend him because I understand people pay him for defending them-it appears to me that the hon. member for Brant was almost in the same classification. He said
that he was opposed to compulsion, and that the opposition group was suggesting compulsion. I could not help wondering if he had ever read P.C. 2246 by which the government is using compulsion to keep men on the farm, using compulsion to say that before a man leaves the farm he must have a permit, and that if he leaves the farm temporarily he must come back. The deputy minister of labour said recently that he proposes to use compulsion to take 200,000 workers out of non-essential industry and put them into agriculture. I am not complaining of that.
I am simply pointing out to the hon. member for Brant that compulsion is already here and that we ought to recognize that fact.
It seems to me that the Minister of Agriculture, as the one who is charged with the responsibility of ensuring that Canada meets its food production commitments, is the one to whom we must look to do his best in the cabinet and1 in its man-power committee te see to it that measures are taken to guarantee sufficient man-power on the farms to enable the farmers to produce what the Minister of Agriculture is asking them to produce.
It is wrong to say that on this side of the house we merely criticize. I think we have offered some suggestions, and offered them repeatedly. One of the suggestions we have offered repeatedly is that something should be done to standardize the calling up of men across Canada for military service. I need not go back into the question of P.C. 2252, passed on the 24th March last. That has been discussed sufficiently in the house already. But I should like to place a table on Hansard, and with the permission of the committee 1 should like to have it appear in Hansard in tabulated form. The table is contained in sessional paper 136F, which was tabled in the house on Monday, April 5, 1943. It deals with this question:
How many men in each military district, as at December 31, 1942, have (a) been called up for military service, (b) have applied for postponement for six months or longer.
The table gives the numbers of men who were called up for military service in the different administrative divisions, the number applying for postponement, and the number of postponements granted, and at the foot of the table appear these two explanatory notes:
"Called up for military service" is deemed to mean that an order vras served on a man pursuant to the national selective service mobilization regulations requiring him to report for military training.

The reason why I draw this to the attention of the minister is that I think here is one of the reasons why the situation has not been very satisfactory. The stand which this

group took a year ago on this whole question of man-power was that we objected to the conscripting of man-power by order in council. One of our reasons was that if you have no law on the statute books, but instead you have orders in council, and quasi-judicial boards set up, these boards have it in their power to say to what extent they will recognize the interpretative letter sent out by the department.
Oh, they have followed it ever since it was sent out.

I can refer the minister to many cases, or if he will look at the files of the deputy minister of labour he will find many eases where it seems to me, at least, that they were still not paying any attention to that interpretative letter.
I think my hon. friend will agree with this, that the mere fact that a person writes to him is not evidence that the facts contained in the letter are correct.

I think he will find that since this interpretative letter was sent out, there is a greater uniformity than before in the application of the policy.

I will say that immediately, that Mr. MacNamara has, in my opinion, done a good job since he has taken over, andi that there has been a 100 per cent improvement. I think one ought to foe very fair about that, and I wish to make that statement here. But that does not alter the fact I stated a moment ago. Many of the cases in which the board refuse to grant postponement have been referred to me. The minister says that does not guarantee that they are right; but when I have referred them to Mr. MacNamara they have been granted postponement, upon his insistence.

Is this not true-I am speaking from my own experience, but I imagine that of other hon. members is pretty much the same-that many of the cases which have been referred to him in the last two or three months are cases which had been dealt with before that letter was sent out? That is, they had been refused postponement earlier, the men had been in camp, in many cases, and there have been some of them removed from camps since, but most of the criticisms are with regard to old actions.

My hon. friend spoke of the director of national selective service "insisting". Any decision made is on the facts, it is not on the insistence of any officers of my department. I think it would be jnfortunate if it got abroad in this country ;hat merely because a member of parliament wrote to an officer of my department the man stood a better chance of deferment than a person who had not got in touch with a member of parliament. I think my hon. friend will agree with that.

Yes; I would be the last person to want to leave that impression. But I say that in a great many cases where the facts made it apparent that a man asking for postponement had a bona fide case, and it had been referred to Mr. MacNamara, and Mr. MacNamara had referred it to the board and had asked for a reconsideration, the case was given reconsideration, and in quite a few cases the man was granted postponement. And I am glad he got it if he deserved it.
With reference to what the Minister of Agriculture has just said, it is true that complaints are not as numerous as they were before the interpretative letter went out. The
interpretative letter has done a great deal of good. But there are two things about that.	There are	still some cases.Mr.	GARDINER: There	are bound to be.

Second, the conduct of the board prior to the interpretative letter has put many of these men in the army, and there is no way of getting them back unless some arrangements can be made	with the	military	authorities.	Unfortunately the interpretative letter was the old case of bolting the stable door after the horse	had gone.
It seems to me that the Minister of Agriculture, as a member of the man-power committee, has a duty to see to it that in the allocation of man-power the regulations which give the right of postponement to men who are essential to agriculture are rigidly adhered to because, if they are not, men will continue to be taken off the farms in places where they are absolutely necessary, and, as has already happened in many cases, older people will leave the farms or, I am afraid, in some cases dispose of their stock and just live on the farm, raising a little bit of garden produce and enough poultry for their own use.
The first thing we have tried to suggest throughout is the standardization of the application of the National Resources Mobilization Act call-up with respect to the different military districts. Up to the present it has not been uniformly or fairly applied in one district as against another, and I am hoping that it will be more uniformly administered as time goes by. I hope, too, that the government will try to find some machinery, other than the type of machinery we have now, under which we have boards with quasi-judicial powers with the result that national selective service finds that it has not complete power to deal with the situation as it feels it ought to be dealt with.
I do not ask this with any critical intent, but has my hon. friend any suggestions along those lines? I should like to have them.

I do not know whether it is too late to do so now or not, but what we advocated last year was that the whole principle of the allocation of man-power should be put in the form of a statute. In the first place we asked that it be centred in one department. As the minister knows, we had a number of different authorities handling this matter. National service called the men; then the army came into the picture; the

Department of Labour looked after one branch, and the Department of Agriculture looked after another.
The hon. member will agree that we are making progress.

That is a step towards progress. I do not mind saying that at all. The provisions for calling men should be in the form of a statute, and these men should have certain definite rules outlined clearly, so that there is not too much discretion left to the board, as is the situation at present, with the result that in some districts where there is a board with certain prejudices or leanings, the regulations are interpreted) in one way, while in another district, with a totally different outlook, the regulations are interpreted differently. Up to date the regulations have been so general that they could be interpreted in any way in which a particular board might care to interpret them.
There have been other sources of man-power. So far as farming is concerned, there is the whole question of conscientious objectors. A return I have here, sessional paper 257, shows about 1,273 conscientious objectors doing alternative service work. Some do fairly useful work in camps clearing the woods, while others are building ski trails and working in national parks, some of which work could very well be left until times of peace. I think most of these conscientious objectors could be put on farms, and I believe the Minister of Labour is taking some steps toward that end.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would point out to the hon. member that it is impossible for us to proceed in an orderly manner if members of the committee discuss two departments at the same time. Hon. members should follow the rules. I am not master of the rules; I must abide by them. I would therefore ask hon. members not to discuss two departments, simultaneously.

I wish to abide by your ruling, Mr. Chairman, but we have been discussing the man-power situation as it applies to agriculture, and I was about to observe that there are 152 conscientious objectors in gaol, many of whom would be much more useful on farms. A number of them were taken off the farms and put in gaol.
I have in mind one with reference to whom I have been in correspondence with various departments of government, but without success. His neighbours write to me stating that his stock is wandering into their yards, and that there is no one to look after his farm. It

seems to me he would be of much greater service on his farm than languishing in gaol at Regina.
The suggestion made by the hon. member for Brant is not a new one. I made it on February 15 to the minister. That suggestion is that the number of men called for military service in Canada-the roster is 60,000-ought to be carefully combed to see if any of these men could be returned to agriculture for a period of time. I think the Minister of Agriculture could make representations to the Department of National Defence, not with the idea of cutting down the army, but to point out that some of these men could very well be spared for a period in the spring and fall. At present a man has to make application, and the discretion lies entirely with his commanding officer. The average commanding officer who has trained a man and fitted him to do useful work round the barracks, or in the particular location where the unit happens to be, will not be keen to let that man go. That stands to reason. If the man-power situation continues to be serious, the Minister of Agriculture might very well make representations to the Department of National Defence and ask that these home defence men be checked over to see if some could not be sent back, particularly next fall, to help take off the crop. I saw a number of anomalous situations last fall. At a time when, throughout Saskatchewan, there were women and young boys in the fields, and they were sending several trainloads of boys in their teens from the east, I went into a training camp in Saskatchewan where there were several thousand husky young men, most of them off the farm. They did not have much equipment and were being given physical drill and route marches to keep them in condition, and within hailing distance there were old people and young people in the fields taking off the crop. It is possible that arrangements could be made next fall to allow a large number of men to be temporarily released to take off the crop. I saw in the press that in Great Britain last fall, while some of the large battleships were being overhauled, the entire crews from his majesty's largest warships were sent o the fields to help the farmers take off the crop. If, being so close to the battle line, the British felt that they could spare these men to gather food, so essential to victory, it seems to me that this government should take into consideration the releasing of men for the same purpose.

Before this item of the estimates carries, there are a few observations I wish to make. Rather than have my silence construed as an indication that we have no

Supply-Agriculture
man-power problem in agriculture in my constituency I feel obliged to say something. In the second place, I am not entirely unmindful of the fact that on a very recent occasion the Minister of Agriculture was more or less instrumental in curtailing a certain debate in which I was engaging at that time.
I am quite in agreement with previous speakers who have asserted that the major problem confronting the farmer to-day is shortage of labour. We can agree most heartily with those who have stated that the depletion of man-power to the armed forces, as well as to industry, has led to that acute labour shortage. In my constituency in Alberta, as I have indicated on previous occasions, we are engaged in a diversified type of agriculture and I know that the farmers there, in common with the farmers in other parts of Canada, have not been in a position to guarantee to labour an attractive wage. It is true that in the proper sense of the word there is no ceiling on farm wages; but in another sense there certainly is, inasmuch as the farmer has had a ceiling placed upon his produce and must consequently place a ceiling upon the wages which he pays farm labour. In effect, therefore, the situation is no different from what it would be if the government had passed an order in council placing a ceiling on farm wages at the level at which they prevail at the present time. The farmer cannot offer regular hours of work per day as can be offered to the worker in industry. After all, we know that circumstances develop on the farm from day to day which may, on occasion, render it necessary for the employee to work sixteen or eighteen hours a day. In a factory the employee is engaged for a period of, let us say. eight or ten hours . a day, and should he engage in overtime he is compensated under most circumstances. We may say that in some instances they pay time and a half for overtime. But that is seldom the situation on the farm, for the simple reason that under the conditions which have prevailed and now prevail the farmer is unable to give any such guarantee. And the same is true with respect to time off. *
While I appreciate the fact that the indus-c trial worker is confronted with many prob-. lems, he does know that he will work so many hours a week on the average. He works so many shifts or so many days, but he knows he will have time off. But on the farm the same work is there every day from early morning until the late hours of the night. During certain seasons of the year, such as the seeding and harvesting seasons, the farmer must take advantage of every possible hour
in order to complete the operation in which he is engaged. These conditions do not tend to attract labour to the farm, especially with the present wages being paid in other industries. We. cannot be unmindful of the fact that if a farm worker has an opportunity of going into the city, especially if he is a young fellow, more particularly if he is single, work there may prove much more attractive than would work in some outlying rural area where the same entertainment was not available.
Farmers all over Canada, and I am speaking more particularly of my own area, who are faced with this labour shortage are not sitting down with folded hands. During the Easter recess I saw a man of eighty-four years of age operating a tractor, and for a full shift too. This illustration could be multiplied many times. At the present time many of our farmers are working as much as twenty hours a day trying to get their crops seeded. It has been indicated by others that the Canadian farmer is an industrious individual, is resourceful, is characterized by his ingenuity; we give him all due credit for that, because if it were not for that he never would have come through the depression years as he did; when he was confronted with the obstacles which confronted him then, he would have thrown up his hands and quit.
One of the things that the farmer objects to more strenuously than anything else is the confusion of red tape and the multitude of orders in council and regulations. He does not know where he stands or what is going to happen to-morrow or next week. During the past winter a large number of farm workers were permitted to take employment in war industry. I thought the number was about
175,000	but I think the minister indicated it as being about 250,000.
The estimate was that about 175,000 would come back in the spring, and about 250,000 left in the fall.

I understand, and I believe the farmer was justified in coming to the same conclusion, that these persons would be obliged to come back to the farm. I tried to put pressure upon the Minister of Labour to have him make a definite statement about the regulations governing these persons who had left agricultural employment to go into factories. I do not wish to say that he was evasive, because that might convey the wrong impression, but he certainly did not answer the question.
Not into factories; into mines and lumbering.

Who had gone out of agriculture; I believe that was the expression I used.
Supply-Agriculture

They had secured permits to leave agriculture to engage in other essential work. I am satisfied that until April 1 the farmer firmly believed that this pool of labour would be directed back to the farm. We now find that there are no regulations which will compel these men to go into that line of work. It is true that if they joined the army services, all was well and good. It was also true that if they remained in industry, they would lose the protection accorded them and come under the National Resources Mobilization Act. I dare say that many of them remained in industry, hoping that in some way or another they might escape the penalty of these regulations.
I recall trying to get a definite answer from the Minister of Labour with respect to those who had gone into industry from the farms and who, after working for a short period, might be regarded or designated as being essential to industry. I rather fancied that in making his reply the minister tried to laugh away the idea that any individual who had spent such a short time in a war industry could be regarded as essential. Yet, if I understood him correctly to-day, he indicated that those who are now regarded as essential to industry would be left there.
Those men did not go to industry at all; they went into the mines and into the lumber camps. They did not go into what is generally called "industry".
It all depends upon what the minister means by the word "industry".
It all depends upon what the public takes out of the term "industry" when it is used in this house.
I honestly believe that if I were to ask the minister to tell me exactly where they went, he would have difficulty in answering the question.

I might have some difficulty in answering the question as to where they all went, but I would not have any difficulty in determining whether they went into industry because they had to get a permit to go.
May I just say this-
May I say to my hon. friend1-

May I comment on this statement first? I have no objection to the Minister of Labour making a statement, but I wish to deal with the statement of the Minister of Agriculture. Not long ago I placed on the order paper a question with

respect to the same matter, and if I am to judge from the information contained in the reply, there is just as much confusion in the government departments with respect to this matter as there is in the minds of farmers who are looking to this pool of labour for assistance.
I do not know whether my hon. friend is a farmer, but-
I have lived in agricultural areas and with farmers all my life and I am capable of making observations.
If my hon. friend is a farmer, the best test would be for him to try to get into industry. He would then see how selective service functions.
May I ask the Minister of Labour what is his definition of "industry"?
It would be more simple if the hon. member would talk about mining and lumbering instead of industry. We would then all understand it.
What is the hon. member talking about?
If the minister does not know what we are talking about, he and the Minister of Agriculture have something in common.
If the hon. member does not know what we are talking about, how can he expect us to understand?
I have given up hope that I would be understood.

I think I have a clear understanding of the word "industry". When you speak of basic industry or mining or lumbering or agriculture, I think I have a 'clear understanding. If my hon. friend wants to lump these all together and call them "industry", I suppose he has a perfect right to do so.
We have such terms as "primary industry" and "secondary industry", and I should like to ask-it is not proper for me to question the minister, because that is contrary to the rules.
That is not contrary to the rules; that is why we are in committee of the whole.

I was referring to the Minister of Labour. I wish to reassert what I said a moment ago, namely, that many farm workers left the farms to engage in essential work. I think that statement is correct. Then we do not have to use the word "industry" at all. The point is that they left agriculture, and we believed they would be directed back to agri-

Supply-Agriculture
cultural employment; I think that was the impression left with the people of this country. Since that time, however, a number of orders in council and regulations have been passed, and we find that the situation is not what we anticipated it would be.
We know, too, that the farmers of Canada are being strangled by numerous restrictions of other types. I am not one of those who are opposed to essential restrictions in war time, but under the guise of war needs these restrictions are often carried to'extremes. I have in mind that in certain instances restrictions with respect to tires and gasoline, and in connection with machine parts, are making it extremely difficult for many of our farmers to carry on, more especially as the shortage of farm hands becomes more acute. It is not my desire to detain the committee, Mr. Chairman, but I believe that one source of farm labour might be discovered if we carried on a complete investigation with respect to the many inspection boards, and boards of other kinds, that have been set up by this government. I do not say that all these people would be qualified to step into agriculture at once, for I understand what evidently a good many people do not understand, that you cannot take an inexperienced individual and send him to a farm to operate the type of machinery that is used in agriculture to-day. I do say, however, that we could take the persons employed by such boards and give them a certain amount of training. There need be no financial loss on their part; in other words, they should not be expected to take a financial loss as a result of that transfer. I believe also that in many communities throughout Canada we could restrict the hours of business in nonessential industries, and on perhaps two days a week-I say this only for purposes of illustration-we might be able to give those people a certain amount of training. No doubt the argument would be advanced that they should not be expected to leave their work for two days a week and lose that income; but, as was indicated by a previous speaker, it might be necessary for the government to step in and subsidize farm wages, so that while such persons were getting experience and assisting on the farm, the farmer would not be obliged to make up the difference between what those persons were being paid previously and what they would receive under this scheme. I think we shall have to give consideration to matters such as these. Then, as a farm worker is taken from agriculture, he might 'be replaced by someone who has obtained at least a minimum of practical experience, and no person should be taken from a farm unless he could be replaced by such an individual.
When we come to the question of taking the boys from the farms, many of our farmers have been driven almost to distraction by the red tape they have tried to clamber over and through in order to have legitimate cases properly considered. I just happen to have a case that I was discussing with one of the government officials to-day. The father, who lives in my constituency, operates 480 acres, with 270 acres under cultivation. He markets from 200 to 300 hogs a year; he has fifty-one head of cattle and thirty-four horses. He operates a diesel tractor, and the only boy he had at home was taken into the army, in spite of the fact that the boy's mother was an invalid and the father is in ill health. I have affidavit after affidavit supporting this boy's claim for release from the army. Incidentally this farmer lost eighty young pigs at one time because he was then unable to do all the work himself. This situation has a detrimental effect upon the farmer concerned, and psychologically it has a most unfortunate effect upon a great many people who know the facts. I say that in such cases, where the legitimacy of the claim is so obvious, we should have some sort of machinery established under which they could be handled with very much less red tape.
There is just one other point I should like to mention. I do not know how true it is, but many of the farmers in my constituency, in commenting upon the production programme of the Minister of Agriculture for 1943, expressed the belief that the minister had looked out over agricultural Canada; that he had seen the vast quantity of feed produced last year, and had concluded that since we had that feed, we would be able to increase the production of hogs, cattle, sheep and so forth during 1943, forgetting, of course, that as the production of live stock is increased, just to that extent the supply of farm labour must be increased. I heard that opinion expressed in a great many quarters. They seemed to believe that the minister had based his 1943 programme upon the fodder production in Canada last year, though I am not saying that is true.
In conclusion, let me say that the farmer will carry on to the very best of his ability. He realizes that food must be produced for the civilian population, the industrial worker and the members of the three armed services in Canada and out of Canada; and, as I stated the other day, he also knows that we have commitments to our allies both for the period of the war and for the post-war years. The farmer considers that Canada is the country to which the rest of the world will be looking for the food supplies that will be so essential
Supply-Agriculture

during the post-war reconstruction period. He will carry on, but I suggest that the warning sign is displayed right now, and that unless we proceed cautiously and give to agriculture the attention it deserves, very shortly we may be confronted with conditions which will have a detrimental effect upon Canada and upon our war effort.

Apparently there is a disposition on the part of members of the government to attach a new meaning to the word "industry". The hon. member for Red Deer was thrown off his line of thought by the insistence of the ministers upon a certain definition of that word. May I give the definition of "industry" as it appears in the dictionary on the table of the house: "Diligence; habitual employment in useful work; * branch of trade or manufacture." If lumbering activity is not a branch of manufacture, I should like to ask the ministers what it is.
That is the adjective the hon. member is talking about?

No; that is the noun. The minister would do well to consult the dictionary once in a while. I have no particular objection to the ordinary free passage of debate. I think it is unfair, though, to have technicalities of that sort brought up to embarrass a member when he is speaking.

There is another matter under the general heading of "administration" in the Department of Agriculture to which I should like to direct the attention of the minister. I had hoped I might be able to bring it to his attention in time, so that he might make some reply to-night. However, I shall call it to his attention, in the hope that he may say something about it later on, during the discussion of the estimates of his department. I refer to the whole question of the use of farm products in an industrial way. I have reference to the production of rubber, and other synthetic materials from products of the farm. This is a matter which is no longer in a theoretical stage, but which is actually capable of being implemented at the present time.

We have gone a long way in avoiding the rules in one direction; I hope we shall not start to avoid them in another. This whole question arises under the discussion of the estimate for the experimental farm. I suggest the matter should be discussed when we reach that item.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Lethbridge will appreciate that, after all, the committee must discuss all the items in the Department of Agriculture. The matter to which the last speaker referred may arise under some other item. I believe the Chair has been lenient in the matter. Prior to the Easter recess the leader of the opposition deplored the fact that he thought there was something lacking in the deliberations of the committees of the house, in that we have a great deal of repetition. When we find an attempt, to-day and yesterday, to discuss two departments at the same time, we run into some difficulties.

I was not implying, Mr. Chairman, that you had not managed the committee wisely. At the same time, however, there is doubt in, my mind as to just how far we can go in discussing this topic. I approve the way in which you have allowed the discussion to drift. My experience has been that hon. members who wish to talk will talk themselves out, and when they talk themselves out, they then allow progress. So that they might as well talk themselves out at one time as another.
Would the Chairman say on which item it would be possible to discuss the industrial use of agricultural products? Would it come under agricultural chemistry?

Work in connection with it is largely carried on at experimental farms. It would be discussed, under the item for experimental farms, or for the administration of science services. A certain part of it would be carried on under that item.

I believe the hon. member for Moose Jaw will have a motion to make in connection with it. Before the committee passes this item, I should like to ask a question. The minister mentioned
175.000	men who have gone from the farms into the mines and logging camps, and who are expected to return. Does that include the 395,000, or is that in addition to the
395.000	who left the farms?

As was stated, that is on the first of March. I stated to-night that that is the time when labour on the farm is low.

I refer to the classification which comes under farm labour, rather than members of farmers' families. That classification is low on March 1. The 250,000 left last fall-or approximately that many. It was expected' that 175,000 at least would return to the farms this spring. They would not be back by March 1. All of them would not be back by that time; some may have been.
Is it the Chairman's opinion that the matter I sought to discuss might be discussed at the points suggested by the minister?
